articles.title: Under-the-radar implication of Dem blue wave means 'zero' chance GOP accomplishes critical goal, experts warn
articles.summary: Ron DeSantis warns that Tuesday's Senate losses effectively end Trump's chances of replacing Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito with conservatives.
articles.body:
Republicans' sweeping losses Tuesday could reshape the Supreme Court for years, prominent conservatives warned, arguing that Democrats' new Senate majority may block President Donald Trump from replacing Justices Clarence Thomas or Samuel Alito with conservative successors.

"Assuming Republicans lose the seats where prediction markets have the Democrats at 90+% to win, that would produce 55 Democrat Senate seats," Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis wrote on X on Tuesday night in a post that was viewed almost 4 million times.

"Chance of confirming a worthy successor to Justice Thomas and/or Alito during President Trump's term: Zero. Chance of confirming a worthy successor during a hypothetical GOP admin 2029-2033: probably zero (GOP won't be able to recapture enough seats in 28)."

Democrats took control of the Senate Tuesday night and hold 54 seats as of midday Wednesday, and DeSantis was joined on social media by several others explaining that Alito, 76, and Thomas, 78, will be almost impossible to replace with equally conservative appointees.

Ed Whelan, a conservative legal expert who clerked for the late Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, wrote on X that Trump is now effectively blocked from appointing federal judges or Supreme Court justices during the final two years of his term.

"If a Republican is elected president in 2028, that president will not be able to appoint any justices or judges until Republicans regain the Senate," Whelan wrote. "Given the deep hole, that might not happen until 2033. "

Whelan also explained that a justice resigning during the upcoming "lame duck" session is highly unlikely and Republicans would have a hard time securing 51 votes.

"If Sherrod Brown wins Ohio seat, he gets sworn into Senate in early December, so Senate becomes 52R-48D," Whelan wrote. "Collins and Murkowski would be unlikely to support anyone Trump would nominate. John Cornyn, Thom Tillis, and Bill Cassidy aren't going to be eager to do Trump any favors. And there are other senators—e.g., John Curtis of Utah—who would be leery of anyone Trump would be eager to push through."

Others on social media echoed similar sentiments.

"In 2033, Clarence Thomas will turn 85 and Samuel Alito will turn 83," conservative author Hans Mahncke posted on X in response to DeSantis. "There is no reason to believe they won't still be going strong on the bench. But the larger point is absolutely valid. No one lives forever, and if these two great men are not eventually replaced by genuinely conservative justices, America will go the way of the rest of the Western world."

"Again, the consequences of tonight's election for the Supreme Court are staggering," Denny Burk, the dean of Boyce College at the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary, posted on X.

articles.title: Nota Legal DF: Confira ganhadores do sorteio e quem levou R$ 1 milhão | G1
articles.standfirst: Morador do Paranoá levou prêmio máximo de R$ 1 milhão em sorteio na tarde desta quinta. Ganhadores tem até fevereiro para indicar dados bancários.
articles.summary: O sorteio do Nota Legal DF premiou 12,6 mil bilhetes com valores de até R$ 1 milhão; ganhadores têm até 4 de fevereiro para indicar dados bancários e resgatar prêmios.
articles.body:
Nota fiscal para uso no Nota Legal no DF — Foto: Secretaria de Economia do DF

Um morador do Paranoá é o ganhador do prêmio máximo no sorteio do Nota Legal, da Secretaria de Economia do Distrito Federal. O sorteio foi realizado na tarde desta quinta-feira (5).

Nessa edição, 12,6 mil bilhetes foram premiados, com valores que vão de R$ 100 a R$ 1 milhão .

O vencedor do prêmio máximo mora no Paranoá e conquistou o prêmio com a compra de um sorvete na Bacio Di Latte do shopping Conjunto Nacional.

Moradores do Setor Leste do Gama e de Presidente Alves, em São Paulo, conquistaram os dois prêmios de R$ 200 mil.

Ganhadores devem informar dados bancários até 4 de fevereiro. Caso o consumidor não informe até a data limite, o valor retorna para o Tesouro do DF.

Estavam aptos a participar compradores que pediram inclusão do CPF na nota fiscal entre novembro de 2025 e abril de 2026.

O coordenador do programa, Mário Cipolli Victer Dias, estima um crescimento de R$ 1 bilhão na arrecadação com a medida.

Segundo o secretário-executivo da Receita da Secretaria de Economia, Clidiomar Soares, o prêmio é uma forma de estimular a justiça fiscal e reduzir sonegações. “Ele transforma um gesto simples do cidadão em justiça fiscal”, pontua.

Após o sorteio, a Secretaria de Economia deve enviar e-mail a todos os vencedores, com informações sobre o prêmio e instruções para o resgate.

O resultado também pode ser conferido no site notalegal.df.gov.br. É possível ingressar na área restrita da plataforma com CPF e senha, caso já tenha cadastro, ou entre com o Gov.br.

Após o login, necessário acessar a aba "Sorteio". Em seguida, o usuário deve selecionar "Sorteio Eletrônico PNL - 2º semestre de 2026" e clicar no "Status" do participante.

articles.title: Erika Hilton tem interesse em disputar eleição para Prefeitura de SP  | G1
articles.standfirst: Deputada recordista de votos mantém conversas com o PT sobre possível mudança de partido. Direção do PSOL afirma que uma candidatura ao Executivo pode ser negociada para manter integrantes na legenda.
articles.summary: Erika Hilton avalia disputar a Prefeitura de São Paulo e negocia com o PT, enquanto o PSOL oferece protagonismo no Executivo para manter a deputada federal.
articles.body:
Deputada Erika Hilton (PSOL - SP) — Foto: Renato Araújo / Câmara dos Deputados

A deputada federal Erika Hilton (PSOL-SP) afirmou que tem interesse em disputar a Prefeitura de São Paulo em uma próxima eleição e que ainda não decidiu se deixará o PSOL para se filiar ao PT. A parlamentar pretende conversar com a direção nacional antes de definir seu futuro partidário.

“Eu tenho pensado bastante sobre a disputa para a Prefeitura em São Paulo também. É uma coisa que eu tenho começado a olhar com certo interesse”, afirmou ao g1 .

A declaração foi dada após a deputada ser questionada sobre a possibilidade de negociar sua permanência no PSOL. Mais cedo, a presidente nacional da legenda, Paula Coradi, disse ao g1 que pretende discutir projetos políticos com Erika e outros integrantes do partido que mantêm conversas com o PT. Segundo Paula, o PSOL estaria disposto a lançar a parlamentar na disputa por um cargo do Executivo.

Questionada sobre a possibilidade de Erika disputar a Prefeitura de São Paulo, Coradi afirmou: “Não há dúvidas sobre a importância da Erika e de que seria uma excelente candidata. O PSOL está, como sempre esteve, aberto a esse diálogo.”

Nos últimos meses, nomes do PSOL como Guilherme Boulos , Natália Boulos, Rick Azevedo, Luciana Genro e a própria Erika têm mantido conversas com a direção do PT. Segundo uma pessoa próxima ao presidente nacional da legenda, Edinho Silva, a filiação dos parlamentares ao partido estaria praticamente acertada, mas ainda dependeria de um entendimento com o PSOL sobre as condições de saída.

Erika, porém, afirma que ainda não tomou uma decisão sobre seu futuro partidário. A deputada admitiu estar “desgostosa” com a condução do processo eleitoral deste ano e com o que considera uma quebra de acordos, mas disse que permanecer no PSOL ainda é uma possibilidade.

“Eu vou conversar com a direção, entender o que está acontecendo. Vou ver se eu vou avançar com as conversas com o PT”, disse.

Em junho, a parlamentar chegou a criticar publicamente o PSOL por, segundo ela, privilegiar candidaturas de pessoas brancas e cisgênero na distribuição de recursos eleitorais para as eleições de 2026 .

A parlamentar afirmou que o contato da direção sobre marcar uma reunião ocorreu nesta semana e que não sabe se uma possível candidatura municipal será abordada nas reuniões. Coradi, por sua vez, disse que os integrantes haviam sido procurados, mas que as conversas ainda não tinham sido marcadas.

Erika foi a mulher mais votada do país para a Câmara dos Deputados, com 1,5 milhão de votos. Apesar das críticas, afirmou que mantém respeito e carinho pelo PSOL e que avalia as condições tanto para sair quanto para permanecer.

“Então, acho que há sempre um caminho, sim, para que o desfecho seja diferente desse que está aparecendo”, afirmou, em referência à possibilidade de deixar o partido.

As possíveis saídas são discutidas após o afastamento entre a direção do PSOL e a Revolução Solidária, corrente ligada a Boulos e da qual Erika faz parte. O grupo defendia uma federação com o PT, proposta derrotada internamente no começo do ano.

Nos bastidores, a avaliação dentro da corrente é que o acordo firmado antes da eleição buscava facilitar a convivência interna, sem estabelecer uma saída posterior. Há, porém, críticas ao que é considerado descumprimento desse entendimento pela direção.

Também provocaram insatisfação as sinalizações, pela imprensa, de que o PSOL dificultaria eventuais desfiliações. Nesse setor, a avaliação é que essas manifestações prejudicam o diálogo.

Segundo relatos reservados à reportagem, o debate sobre os próximos passos envolve parlamentares e militantes e ainda está no início. A defesa de uma atuação mais unificada da esquerda é um dos argumentos apresentados pelo grupo.

articles.title: Democrat poised to flip deep-red House seat without airing a single TV ad
articles.summary: Victoria Broderick and Cyril Jefferson lead GOP incumbents in deep-red districts after running remarkably low-cost campaigns.
articles.body: Two years after losing to Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais by 43 points, Democrat Victoria Broderick is leading in his deep-red Tennessee district by just 280 votes in the state’s unofficial final results — despite spending under $100,000 and airing no paid TV ads. If her lead holds, the result would end DesJarlais’ 16-year congressional career. First elected in 2010, the Republican was seeking his ninth term in a district President Donald Trump carried by 24 points in 2024. The latest FEC figures available before Election Day show DesJarlais’ campaign spent $508,166 through Oct. 14, compared with just $90,062 for Broderick. His campaign also raised more than seven times as much as hers — $667,181 to $94,217 — yet the longtime incumbent is trailing in the deep-red seat. REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES Axios reported, citing AdImpact, that Broderick’s campaign had no record of airing paid television ads. Instead, she credited a grassroots operation that had been building for more than two years. Broderick was not the only Democrat threatening to pull off a low-dollar House upset. Axios also highlighted a similar race in North Carolina, where High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson currently leads Republican Rep. Addison McDowell 51.1% to 48.9%. Axios reported, citing AdImpact, that Jefferson had no tracked advertising spending, although a separate tracker lists $2,000 in Google ads, including YouTube placements. LEE CARTER: THE 5 WORDS THAT EXPLAIN THIS ELECTION BETTER THAN ANY COMMERCIAL McDowell had won the district by 38.3 points in 2024, according to election results. Broderick told Axios that her apparent upset was not a surprise to her team. "I know it was a shock for the rest of the country, but it wasn’t a shock for our team," she said. Jefferson similarly credited volunteers, saying, "You have to go engage them." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Wake Forest University political science professor John Dinan told local news outlet WFDD that challengers in such a Republican-leaning district would normally need "a lot of TV ads and a lot of money," but "there wasn’t a whole lot of money spent." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The two races showed how grassroots organizing and strong local candidates can make traditionally Republican districts competitive despite major financial disadvantages. articles.title: How MAGA lost the midterms: Failure to acknowledge reality
articles.summary: Too many Republicans refused to call a spade a spade, treating anyone who disagreed with the president as an outcast.
articles.body:
All across the nation, Republicans are reeling from a series of losses that can only be described as seismic. Midterm elections have traditionally proven unfavorable for the party occupying the Oval Office, but this election was clearly a referendum on Trumpian populist politics.

In Texas, Republicans lost a Senate seat after Trump primaried a sitting senator who disagreed with him, for the benefit of an official who had, among other things, been rejected by members of his own party. This cleared the way for a Democrat who distorts Scripture to fit his own narrative.

In South Carolina , Republicans lost another Senate seat because nepotism doesn’t serve as a cover for experience. In North Carolina , Republicans surrendered yet another seat after the president backed a political operative who made an inauthentic attempt to portray himself as a champion of rural North Carolina values, despite having spent the better part of 20 years working in the polished corridors of Washington.

While some Republicans enjoyed the glistening ballrooms of political power, they failed to acknowledge honestly and publicly the sticker shock being felt by their constituents. The trade war drove up the cost of goods . The ongoing conflict in Iran has driven up gas prices and the administration has failed spectacularly to communicate a clear objective for American involvement in the conflict. Housing prices remain unsustainably high , putting homeownership increasingly beyond the reach of the average American.

Meanwhile, Trump has remained preoccupied with architectural ambitions: adding gold to nearly every crevice of the White House, constructing a presidential helipad , building a ballroom that dwarfs the White House, planning to erect a golden arch in Washington and adding his own name to the Kennedy Center.

Americans, however, are not stupid. Democrats simply capitalized on reality. For Republicans, this was a modern-day Marie Antoinette situation: “Let them eat cake.”

Republicans also squandered their opportunity to deliver good governance. While H.R.1 , the “Big Beautiful Bill,” represented a significant legislative victory, internal divisions brought much of the legislative progress promised to Americans in 2024 to a grinding halt.

Those feuds spilled into public view, exposing a clear fissure within the Republican Party primarily centered around a president seemingly incapable of working with those who disagree with him. Elon Musk, Tucker Carlson, Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) and others have all , at one point or another, drawn the ire of the president, and have fractured the Republican Party.

In addition, several campaign promises from the 2024 election remain unfilled. The Russia-Ukraine War has not ended. Inflation has not subsided . Healthcare reform has stalled. Energy prices are rising . The Department of Education still exists. Americans received no Department of Government Efficiency “DOGE” dividend . No national proof of citizenship requirement has been enacted.

Unfulfilled, stalled and altered promises have simply eroded trust in Trump’s party.

It must also be noted that a major campaign message from Republicans was avoiding accountability. Administration officials campaigned across the country warning that Democrats, upon regaining control of the House and Senate, would immediately turn their attention toward investigating Republicans. This provided Democrats with fuel for accountability. Such campaign messaging was tone deaf to the economic reality Americans are facing each day.

Ultimately, the danger of a populist movement is that it can render political parties spineless and strip them of their true character. Too many Republicans refused to call things what they are, treating anyone who disagreed with the president as an outcast.

Unity should never mean uniformity. When a chief executive goes unquestioned, Republicans eventually discover that the American public is quite willing to hold them accountable. Perhaps most dangerous of all, this political philosophy stands in direct opposition to one of America’s most enduring principles: the free expression of ideas.

Republicans would be wise to take this moment seriously as they begin preparing for 2028. Americans are so fed up with the current political establishment that they appear increasingly willing to send candidates espousing socialist ideologies to Congress rather than elect another Republican. That should be a sobering realization for a party that prides itself on individual liberty, economic opportunity and principled leadership.

Pastor Xavier Kelley is a licensed Baptist minister and former private school teacher.

articles.title: Jesse Watters: GOP coalition ‘totally collapsed’
articles.summary: Fox News’s Jesse Watters said Wednesday the Republicans’ election coalition fell apart in this year’s midterms, with Democrats winning both the House and Senate. “If you’re going to make people who are young, struggling, living paycheck to paycheck, have to pay more for stuff and make it harder for them to climb the ladder, it’s…
articles.body:
Fox News’s Jesse Watters said Wednesday the Republicans’ election coalition fell apart in this year’s midterms, with Democrats winning both the House and Senate.

“If you’re going to make people who are young, struggling, living paycheck to paycheck, have to pay more for stuff and make it harder for them to climb the ladder, it’s not going to go well,” Watters said on Fox News’s “The Five.”

“The only people he really won are people over 65, and those are people who have a home, invested in the stock market, and can kind of see the big picture, but the coalition’s totally collapsed,” he added, referencing President Trump. “I mean, we lost whites, whites. You can’t do that, if you’re a Republican. Men, Hispanics, big time, and so it’s going to take a while to put the coalition back together because it was in the heartland.”

Watters’s comments follow a rough Election Day for Republicans, in which the party lost both chambers of Congress and struggled in places where they were historically successful.

Democrats are projected to grow their caucus in the House from 214 members to 262 , while their Senate caucus is projected to grow from 47 members to 55 , according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Republicans faced an uphill battle in this year’s elections, with concerns about the cost of living, Trump’s struggling approval rating and the unpopular war in Iran creating obstacles for the GOP.

According to a polling average from DDHQ, Trump’s approval rating a day before the midterms was at 38.4 percent , while his disapproval rating was 58.7 percent.

Trump’s policy for the next two years will most likely face hurdles from the incoming Democratic Congress, a massive shake-up in the relationship dynamic between the legislative and executive branches in Washington, D.C.

articles.title: Houchin challenges McClain for House GOP conference chair
articles.summary: Rep. Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) is challenging House GOP conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) for the role, which will be central as Republicans work to sharpen their messaging in the minority next year and counter Democrats’ agenda heading into 2028. Houchin said in a “Dear Colleague” letter to Republicans on Wednesday that the road back to…
articles.body:
Rep. Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) is challenging House GOP conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) for the role, which will be central as Republicans work to sharpen their messaging in the minority next year and counter Democrats’ agenda heading into 2028.

Houchin said in a “Dear Colleague” letter to Republicans on Wednesday that the road back to the Republican majority “runs through our message and our ability to communicate it effectively.”

“I am a communications professional,” Houchin said. “Before coming to Congress, I ran my own public relations business. I have run campaigns from the local to the national level. I have a Master’s degree in political management and am a graduate of the Women’s Campaign School at Yale.”

“I’ve spent over twenty years in public relations, communications, and campaigns. Now, I’m running for Chair of the House Republican Conference to put that experience to work for all of you,” she added.

Houchin serves on the House Rules Committee, the House Budget Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

McClain, meanwhile, said in her own “Dear Colleague” letter that Tuesday’s elections were a “devastating setback” for the Republican conference.

“I will not minimize the magnitude of this defeat. While we’ve been knocked down, we are ready to get back in the fight,” she added. “We have an opportunity to chart a new course while building on the relationships, experience, and momentum we’ve experienced together.”

She argued that if she’s reelected, she would “take the fight to the Democrats, expose their radical agenda, and offer Americans an inspirational vision for the future under Republican leadership.”

In a post on the social platform X , McClain touted endorsements from 33 House Republicans, including House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole (R-Okla.) and House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair James Comer (R-Ky.), as well as two GOP candidates who were elected to Congress this cycle.

articles.body:
A New York state appeals court panel will hold oral arguments Thursday on President Trump’s bid to overrule the jury’s verdict finding him guilty on 34 counts of criminally falsifying business records to conceal a hush money payment during his 2016 campaign.

Trump argues that jurors improperly saw evidence protected by presidential immunity and prosecutors’ theory of the case is preempted by federal campaign finance law. He also says his trial judge should’ve recused himself and gave bad instructions to the jury.

The president is separately attempting to move his appeal to federal court, a push being handled separately that has so far fallen flat .

The five-judge panel on the Appellate Division, First Judicial Department will take the bench at noon EST.

Trump is at the White House, according to his daily schedule, and is not expected to attend.

articles.title: Hegseth faces bipartisan impeachment threat after Iran war gets blame for GOP midterm slaughter
articles.summary: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth faces a bipartisan impeachment threat as House Republicans say a privileged resolution could pass when Congress returns.
articles.body: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is facing a bipartisan impeachment threat when Congress returns next week as Republicans seethe over their devastating losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. Bipartisan frustration over the war in Iran, quietly simmering for months, is now openly erupting after Democrats stunned the country with historic victories in the House and Senate. That anger could all now hit Hegseth, with several House Republicans telling Fox News Digital that they believe a resolution to impeach him could pass as early as next week. "He's screwed," one House GOP lawmaker told Fox News Digital. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a longtime critic of foreign intervention by the U.S., told Fox News Digital he intends to force a vote on impeaching Hegseth when Congress returns if the Pentagon chief does not resign first. GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH He'll do so by filing a privileged resolution, a mechanism aimed at getting a vote on legislation despite opposition from the majority party's leaders. Once a privileged resolution is filed, lawmakers have two legislative days to hold a vote. 7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS But the procedure notably carries two steps. Before a vote on the measure itself, leaders can call up a vote to "table" the bill or refer it to the relevant committee, which in both instances effectively kills it. That procedural vote is normally where most privileged resolutions die. But in this case, several House Republicans told Fox News Digital they believe the impeachment resolution could ultimately be successful. GOP LAWMAKER SAYS MORE QUALIFIED OFFICIALS SHOULD LEAD PENTAGON, QUESTIONS HEGSETH'S 'MORAL COMPASS' "If he introduces it, it'll pass," a second House Republican told Fox News Digital. Two more said they expected the same. One GOP lawmaker said attendance could be a key factor in impeaching Hegseth. It's highly possible that many Republicans who lost re-election simply do not return for the final two months of the year, that person said. And with just a razor-thin majority, only a handful of absences would be enough for Hegseth to get impeached if all Democrats stuck together. The Fox News Decision Desk projected Democrats taking the House shortly before midnight on Tuesday. Projections showed that the war in Iran, along with tariff policies, were key drivers in voters turning their backs on the GOP. And while President Donald Trump told reporters he believes Hegseth is doing "a good job," people in his circle appear to have their knives out. "Hegseth is on the chopping block," a former White House official told Fox News Digital. A current White House official said, "[Tuesday] would have looked very different without the Iran war. I believe you’ll ultimately see [Trump] hold Pete Hegseth accountable and that will play out in the lame duck." ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH But the White House criticized the potential impeachment push on Thursday. "As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. And another White House official said, "If crazed Democrats want to abuse their power and politicize their process of investigations, subpoenas, and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers." Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell on Wednesday dismissed rumors that Trump could get rid of Hegseth himself. "Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists. The Department of War has followed the law and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America," he told Fox News Digital. It's also worth noting that the majority of House Republicans will still oppose impeaching Hegseth — and many are still skeptical. CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES "I really doubt [it]," another House Republican told Fox News Digital. "Depends on if anyone wants to flip off the president walking out the door." There is likely to be healthy support on the other side of the aisle for such a push as well. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker, has consistently criticized Hegseth. He posted on X Thursday morning, "Why is Pete Hegseth still around?" Even more moderate Democrats have signaled their support, given the administration did not seek the consent of Congress at any point during the ordeal. Adam Smith, D-Wash., who is expected to take over leadership of the House Armed Services Committee next year, told CNN's "This Morning" last month. If Hegseth were impeached, he would not be removed before a trial in the U.S. Senate. Fox News Digital reached out to the committee's Republican majority and the Pentagon for comment.

articles.title: Warren says populist economic messaging drove Democratic victories
articles.summary: Progressive Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) on Thursday chalked up Democrats’ resounding midterm victories to populist messaging on the economy. “Anyone seeking to understand the midterm’s lessons should start here: Democrats won by being populist economic fighters who were unafraid to call out the corrupt politicians and corporate interests who have rigged the system at the…
articles.body:
Progressive Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) on Thursday chalked up Democrats’ resounding midterm victories to populist messaging on the economy.

“Anyone seeking to understand the midterm’s lessons should start here: Democrats won by being populist economic fighters who were unafraid to call out the corrupt politicians and corporate interests who have rigged the system at the expense of everyone else,” Warren wrote on social platform X .

Democrats saw a seismic victory Tuesday, flipping the Senate and House and relegating congressional Republicans to the minority for the rest of President Trump’s time in office .

Decision Desk HQ has called 251 House seats and 54 Senate seats in favor of Democrats, with multiple close results still outstanding.

Democrats this cycle capitalized on Americans’ frustrations with the cost of living. Inflation has risen above 3.5 percent amid the Iran war , which has pushed up gas and grocery prices.

Nearly 9 in 10 voters told NBC News that the cost of living was either a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote, with more than 7 in 10 voters saying the economy is in either “not so good” or “poor” condition.

Those frustrations gave Democrats an opening in traditional conservative strongholds, with Adam Hamilton in Kansas , Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico in Texas becoming the first Democrats elected to the Senate from their respective states since 1934, 1988 and 1998, respectively.

Talarico, along with Democratic candidates such as Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan , campaigned on limiting the influence of billionaires and corporations on politics and strengthening unions. El-Sayed also made Medicare for All a central tenet of his Senate bid.

Warren, in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee, expanded on her view of the elections in a Time magazine op-ed , writing Democrats “won by recognizing Americans’ economic pain” and by “pledging to upend this system.”

“Across the country, Democrats stood up for big policy changes like increasing the federal minimum wage, expanding child care, reining in Big Tech, data centers, and AI, and reforming health care,” she wrote.

articles.title: Democrat Scott Colom adds to lead in Mississippi Senate ballot counting
articles.summary: The Democrat in Mississippi’s Senate race expanded his narrow lead over the incumbent senator Wednesday, possibly giving Democrats yet another seat to pad their majority. Democrat Scott Colom now leads Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) by just more than 1,800 votes, according to Decision Desk HQ, with a smattering of remaining ballots being slowly added by…
articles.body:
The Democrat in Mississippi’s Senate race expanded his narrow lead over the incumbent senator Wednesday, possibly giving Democrats yet another seat to pad their majority.

Democrat Scott Colom now leads Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) by just more than 1,800 votes, according to Decision Desk HQ, with a smattering of remaining ballots being slowly added by counties around the state.

Colom’s campaign manager Gerard Henderson said on the social platform X that the campaign is “confident” their lead will grow as more ballots are counted.

“We’re confident Scott’s lead will continue to grow as the remaining votes are counted. We’re staying focused and protecting the integrity of our election,” Henderson wrote .

Mail ballots will continue to arrive in Mississippi for up to five days after the election so long as they were postmarked by Election Day.

Mississippi’s top election official said the state is waiting on 3,600 outstanding ballots to see if they show up in time — far more ballots than the margin between the two candidates.

The remaining votes are not likely to give either candidate a comfortable lead, but Mississippi has no method for a candidate to request a recount under state law. A state election law expert told The Hill that the losing candidate would have to make the case for a recount to a judge and that there is no guarantee one would be granted.

When ballots can arrive in Mississippi was the subject of a Supreme Court decision earlier this year, in which the court ruled against the Republican National Committee and said federal law permitted Mississippi to allow ballots to arrive after the election if they were postmarked in time.

Should Colom pull off a victory in the Magnolia State, he would be the first Black senator elected there since Reconstruction.

Former President Biden previously nominated Colom to be a federal judge in the Northern District of Mississippi, but Hyde-Smith blocked him from having a confirmation hearing, a power home-state senators have over judicial appointments.

Three years later, Colom may come back to defeat Hyde-Smith.

Flipping Mississippi would add to Democrats’ haul in the Senate, where they have already picked up seven seats and have a shot at an eighth or ninth with votes in Alaska also still being counted.

If Democrats win the Senate races in both Mississippi and Alaska, they would win 56 Senate seats for the first time since 2008.

articles.title: Did Vance clear postmidterm message with Trump?
articles.summary: 🎀 Plus: Nicki Minaj is active on X {beacon} It’s Thursday. There are still major races to be called and midterm aftermath to deal with. Luckily, you’re reading this. In today’s issue: Vance’s midterm post-mortem Hegseth in trouble Still counting Mississippi… First lady’s ceasefire Programming note: We’re Claire Leibowitz and Abigail Walker, filling in…
articles.body:
It’s Thursday . There are still major races to be called and midterm aftermath to deal with. Luckily, you’re reading this.

Programming note : We’re Claire Leibowitz and Abigail Walker, filling in for Cate today. Please send me your tips, comments and story ideas to cleibowitz@thehill.com and awalker@thehill.com .

The White House says the president gave his OK to Vice President Vance’s statement on Wednesday blaming massive midterm losses squarely on the Iran War.

Two sources told the that the vice president fired the message without running it by Trump. A White House official told The Hill’s Julia Manchester that Vance flagged it and got it cleared prior to sending.

And two people and a senior White House official told Politico that Vance gave a heads-up before pushing the 614-word post out.

But what does Trump think?: The president had partially blamed the Iran war for the GOP’s losses on Wednesday, but he said he would have done it again.

Trump told The Wall Street Journal that the Middle East conflict “was a piece of it” in an election night interview.

Asked later Tuesday about Vance’s post and whether he knew it was coming, Trump said: “I know how he feels about [the Iran war]. I think it was fine. I thought it was good.”

Those close to Vance see his post as an attempt to distance himself from the Iran war and a signal that he’s looking to take over the American Right, reportedly.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could be facing impeachment, even before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) posted on X Thursday morning that his own Hegseth impeachment resolution is “a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress. They’ll have hearings and trials.”

Hegseth’s ousting of top generals from the military, along with his culture crusade and concerns over the Iran war, have put him in hot water with Democrats and Republicans alike. Massie previously introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September.

Trump defended Hegseth Thursday morning and said he intends to keep him in the role. But he did acknowledge it would be easier to confirm someone new before Democrats take control of Congress.

Trump said he’s received calls from people who are concerned about Hegseth but noted he didn’t “understand why.”

And on Wednesday, the president said Hegseth would be “very popular” if he was elected to replace Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), who opted to run for governor instead of reelection.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) blamed the president for the GOP’s epic midterm defeat.

“This midterm, no question, was a rebuke of the president and the Congress by Democrats, independents and some Republicans that crossed over,” DeSantis said in an interview with Fox News’s Laura Ingraham, adding that a lot of Republican voters stayed home on Tuesday.

“That’s just a fact. They were promised big things, and they didn’t deliver it,” the governor continued.

Exit polling placed economic issues as the primary concern for voters, who ousted Republican leadership across historically red states in districts.

Florida, however, remained largely in GOP control with Sen. Ashley Moody defeating challenger Angie Nixon for Senate and Republican Byron Donalds winning his race to replace DeSantis as governor.

Meanwhile in Texas , the GOP had a tough night.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) wrote in a lengthy social media post on X Wednesday evening that “Texas is blue. That is a hard sentence to utter. But Texas, today at least, is blue.”

The senator described Tuesday’s results as an “impressive victory” for Democrats but warned that “Texans will be hurt.”

“Their assault on business will make Texas a much less attractive place to start or grow a small business,” Cruz added. “Texas will become more like California if they succeed in halting all new investment into AI.”

The results of the Mississippi Senate race have yet to be decided, and with no recount procedure set in place, the results could go to the courts .

Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom are nearly tied in the race to represent Mississippi in the upper chamber with Colom ahead by fewer than 2,000 votes as of Wednesday evening .

The count is still ongoing — in Mississippi, main-in ballots are counted if they are postmarked by Election Day and received within 5 business days. That leaves 3,600 mail-in votes, as well as an additional 15,000 provisional ballots remaining.

Things might get complicated if the race head to a recount, a process decided at the state-level.

As The Hill’s Sophie Brams and Zach Schonfeld write, “When it comes to federal offices like the U.S. Senate, nothing in Mississippi law provides an express way to contest the general election. It effectively leaves it up to judges to determine how disputes are resolved in any push by either side.”

Both candidates have acknowledged the tight race to their supporters.

“We are going to make sure every single vote has been counted, and I am confident we will ultimately flip this seat,” Colom wrote in a post on the social platform X.

“I’ll tell you the Democrats got out and worked, they really got out and worked, and a lot of them showed up today. But not enough of them. I’ll just tell you that right now,” Hyde-Smith said, per Mississippi Today.

“I assure you I will continue to be your U.S. senator,” the GOP candidate added.

Democrats may in part have their sharp rebuke of data centers to thank for their dominance in the 2026 midterm elections.

“Midterm voters both rejected industry-backed candidates and overwhelmingly backed resolutions to halt data center construction, dealing a major blow to the sector,” write The Hill’s Miranda Nazzaro and Rachel Frazin .

In states such as Ohio and Texas, where Democrats pulled off victories by wider margins than expected, voters expressed concern about the construction of data centers.

The GOP was aware of the risk, with the National Republican Senatorial Committee cautioning that data centers could be an “anchor hanging around” Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-Ohio) neck.

In perhaps one of the most surprising signs of Tuesday’s blue wave, a Democrat who dropped out of his race for the Iowa state House still won the contest.

Eric Armstrong defeated Republican candidate Kieth Jones by 9 points, per The Associated Press.

The kicker? Armstrong suspended his campaign in September, citing health issues.

“Because I must prioritize my health and recovery at this time, I am stepping down from my campaign, effective immediately,” Armstrong wrote in a Sept. 7 post on Facebook. “This was a deeply difficult choice. However, I know it is the right one.”

Despite quitting , Armstrong won over voters, beating his Republican opponent by 865 votes, according to AP.

In a Wednesday morning call with The New York Times, the winner said he’d represent his district to the best of his ability.

“But I still have health issues, that’s what I’m struggling with,” Armstrong continued.

Explore 2026 election results, voting trends and historical comparisons with Decision Desk HQ, available through The Hill Insider Premium.

First lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian representatives at the White House to discuss the localized ceasefire in the front-line city Oleshky.

“People experienced the simple joys of life for the first time since 2022,” she said. “Food, clean water and medicine entered the area, and nearly 800 people left their homes in search of safety, loved ones and a renewed sense of being.”

She secured a ceasefire in the region late last month that ended on Sunday.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) said on Thursday that he supported Trump’s plan to stop aid to Israel. “I agree with him on that,” El-Sayed said on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe.”

Former Trump staffer Caroline Sunshine said on Wednesday that Susie Wiles should resign as White House chief of staff, arguing that the GOP’s historic midterm failure was partially her doing and citing unsuccessful messaging strategies.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) responded to Vance’s post-election analysis blaming the blue wave on the unpopular Iran war, writing on social media that the vice president was merely trying to “cover [himself].”

articles.title: Race for Golden’s open House seat in Maine heads to ranked choice voting
articles.summary: The race for the Maine House seat represented by outgoing Rep. Jared Golden (D) is headed to ranked choice voting, the Maine secretary of state’s office announced Thursday. The office noted Republican candidate Paul LePage received 170,263 votes, just shy of 50 percent, while Democrat Matt Dunlap received 164,845 votes, roughly 48 percent. There were…
articles.body:
The race for the Maine House seat represented by outgoing Rep. Jared Golden (D) is headed to ranked choice voting, the Maine secretary of state’s office announced Thursday.

The office noted Republican candidate Paul LePage received 170,263 votes, just shy of 50 percent, while Democrat Matt Dunlap received 164,845 votes, roughly 48 percent. There were more than 6,000 blank votes and 123 votes for write-in candidates.

Because no candidate received more than half of the vote outright during the first round, the race for Maine’s 2nd District will head to ranked choice voting, which the office said will begin Monday.

LePage claimed an early victory even though no call has been made.

“The first step in the process will to be to verify the vote totals from every municipality to ensure accuracy,” Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows (D) said in a statement. “Once the election night totals are verified, assuming neither candidate received a majority of the votes, which is what we are observing now, we will proceed to the ranked choice voting tabulation.”

Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said he had been in contact with Bellows and reiterated that the former Maine governor was still the winner of the Maine House district.

“I have spoken with Secretary of State Bellows and we are aware initial indications show a small number of blank votes and write-ins for this race may trigger Ranked Choice Voting based on their interpretation of law,” Littlefield said in a statement . “It is very clear from our campaign team’s work yesterday talking one-on-one with local town clerks, and the publicly available numbers, that Paul LePage is the Congressman-Elect.”

The Hill has reached out to Dunlap’s campaign for comment.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states to use ranked choice voting statewide.

Voters are asked to rank their choices for the office. If no candidate gets the majority of first-choice votes, the lowest-scoring candidate is eliminated and the results are retallied, using the second choice from voters whose first pick was knocked out.

Maine’s system was implemented in 2018 after voters approved it on a 2016 ballot measure .

President Trump won Golden’s district by 9 percentage points in 2024 , making it one of Democrats’ most vulnerable seats to protect during the midterms.

Decision Desk HQ has already projected that Democrats will win back the House and are poised to win more than 250 seats, though a handful of races have yet to be called.

Julia Mueller contributed . Updated at 12:57 p.m. EST.

articles.title: Ohio's most popular midterm Republican says election results hold a warning for Dems
articles.summary: Frank LaRose says the Republican Party must refocus on human freedom and free market principles after GOP candidates struggled on Election Day.
articles.body: Ohio's most popular midterm Republican says his party needs to refocus its message into a constructive appeal to voters if the GOP hopes to regain the ground it lost on Election Day. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose won his race to become Ohio State Auditor on Tuesday night, securing over 2.3 million votes, a total that easily eclipsed any other statewide Republican candidate. Gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy secured just over 2 million votes in his race, and Sen. Jon Husted secured just under 2.1 million votes in his bid for re-election. FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM' "There are, of course, cycles to American politics, but also I think we as a party need to focus on what we're for, not just what we're against," LaRose told Fox News Digital in an interview. "I mean, we know what we're against. The other side has a bunch of crazy ideas that are dangerous for the future of our states and our nation, but we need to get back to talking about what we're for. We're the party that stands for human freedom, that idea that we're endowed by our Creator with rights, those don't come from government." "Protecting human freedom, protecting free market principles that people can prosper by, you know, the sweat of their own brow and working hard to build a business, those are really kind of the bread and butter conservative issues that drove me to become a Republican when I first started thinking about politics as a young man myself," he continued. FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS LaRose went on to point to Ohio Issue 3, a ballot measure requiring Ohio voters to present voter ID when casting their ballots. The overwhelmingly Republican-backed measure sailed through Tuesday's election with over 65% of the vote, even as Republican candidates struggled. LaRose argued that the measure presents a warning to the midterm election's victorious Democrats that Republican policies remain popular even if candidates fail in their messaging. TRUMP COUNTRY SEES 20-YEAR GOP GRIP ON GOVERNOR'S MANSION SHATTERED "Candidly, I wish more conservatives had showed up to vote yesterday, and I think the outcome might have come out a little different. But even among most people that consider themselves Democrats in Ohio, it doesn't compare to Democrats on the coast, right? The East Coast and the West Coast is more of that kind of, you know, woke DEI cuckoo wing of the party. But even in Ohio, most Democrats are pretty common sense people, and of course, showing your ID to vote is common sense," LaRose said. "Let this be a message to my friends from the other side of the aisle that won their elections in Ohio. Remember that Ohio is not a far left state when it comes to common sense kind of things," he added. "Govern like a Midwestern Democrat and maybe you'll be all right, but if you govern like a coastal Democrat, then I think your time in office is going to be short." POLLSTERS MISSED THE MARK AGAIN — BUT THIS TIME, IT WASN'T REPUBLICANS THEY UNDERESTIMATED As Ohio's secretary of state, LaRose had a front-row seat as election tallies started mounting. He said it became clear with around 60% of the vote tallied that Republicans were not going to have a good night. Nevertheless, he thanked Ohio's 40,000 election workers for their professionalism throughout the election process. LaRose has served as Ohio's elections chief for eight years, and he says his move to state auditor will allow him to keep Ohio's politicians accountable for their spending. articles.title: Hannity calls for public input on future of immigration enforcement
articles.summary: Fox News host Sean Hannity in a recent segment called for the input of the American people on “what they want and what they don’t want” in terms of immigration enforcement. “If you’re like me, you want border security, it’s already happened. Donald Trump achieved that,” Hannity said on Fox News. “He achieved a secure…
articles.body:
Fox News host Sean Hannity in a recent segment called for the input of the American people on “what they want and what they don’t want” in terms of immigration enforcement.

“If you’re like me, you want border security, it’s already happened. Donald Trump achieved that,” Hannity said on Fox News . “He achieved a secure border.”

“It’s time to just ask the American people what they want and what they don’t want in terms of enforcement moving forward,” he added.

Hannity’s remarks come as Democrats seized control of the House and the Senate during a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, securing major wins in battleground states like Texas, Iowa, Maine, Michigan and Ohio.

On Wednesday , Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a social media post that “ Deportations will continue .”

The Trump administration’s crackdown on immigration had been a central topic of conversation and debate ahead of the midterm elections. Democrats across the country have campaigned against the crackdown with some even calling to abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

In the weeks leading up to Election Day, the administration also escalated its efforts to stop noncitizens from voting in the midterms, with states like California and Washington coming under federal scrutiny for potentially having noncitizen voters in their respective states.

Mullin on Election Day posted on social platform X warning noncitizens against voting illegally.

“Illegal voter registration and illegal voting carry significant penalties of up to 5 years in prison and $250,000 maximum fine. Even if you have lawful immigration status—noncitizens who illegally vote are subject to deportation,” Mullin wrote in his post.

Federal law dictates that only U.S. citizens are permitted to vote in federal elections, according to a fact sheet from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

With recent moves like regulatory changes to H-1B visas , plans to revoke 200,000 temporary visas and increased ICE presence in sanctuary cities across the country, the Trump administration has continued to ramp up its efforts on cracking down on immigration.

articles.title: New Jersey mayor who charged at resident during council meeting concedes election loss
articles.summary: Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini was decisively defeated in a mayoral race following the spectacle at a township council meeting last month.
articles.body: The Republican New Jersey mayor who was physically restrained while charging toward a resident during a Pemberton Township council meeting last month has conceded the mayoral race to his Democratic opponent. Mayor Matthew Bianchini congratulated Belinda Fontanez in a Facebook post Wednesday. "The voters of Pemberton Township have spoken, and the results are clear. I offer Belinda Fontanez my sincere congratulations on her victory. As she prepares to take on the responsibility of leading our community, she has my full support for a smooth transition," Bianchini wrote. "I care deeply about the future of this township, and its success matters far more than any single election," he added. Bianchini was decisively defeated, earning just over 30% of the vote, according to unofficial results. 'I BASICALLY SNAPPED': NEW JERSEY MAYOR CHARGES AT RESIDENT DURING CHAOTIC COUNCIL MEETING Bianchini, who was tapped to serve as mayor following the resignation of his predecessor, will remain in the role until the end of this year. Video footage from an October Pemberton Township council meeting captured the mayor being restrained as he sought to advance toward resident Michael Sawka after Sawka appeared to give the middle-finger gesture at the mayor. "I am f---in' gettin' you!" Bianchini can be heard declaring as another individual intervening in the tense situation pushed the mayor back. "I should not have said that," Bianchini told WPVI, adding that it "was wrong" and that he is "not gonna get anybody." NEW JERSEY PRE-K AIDE FACES 61 CHARGES, ACCUSED OF FILMING HIMSELF SEXUALLY ASSAULTING STUDENTS AT SCHOOL "I will not apologize for my actions last night. If you attack my family, as that resident did last night, I will act," the mayor wrote on Facebook, according to the New York Post. The Philadelphia Inquirer reported the mayor's wife, who was in the audience during the meeting, noted in a Facebook comment on a Pine Barrens Tribune post, "I am not condoning my husbands [sic] actions but I will say as a parent and a spouse, I get his protection mode." "He was saying verbally abusive comments about my wife and my daughter," Matthew Bianchini alleged to the Pine Barrens Tribune. "And then he did a hand gesture and looked at my daughter. To me, it appeared like he gave her the finger and that is when I stood up. He looked at me, smiled and gave me the finger and that is when I went out after him." Bianchini and Sawka have a history of bad blood between them. The mayor told WPVI, "I just basically snapped," noting, "I hate to put it this way, but ... it's a long time coming." "Was it wrong? Absolutely. Was it justified? Absolutely. And I would do it again if I had to," the mayor told the outlet. "His family, his stepdaughter, his stepson, his daughter, they all attack me online, and they just come after me just with personal attacks," Sawka told WPVI. Bianchini alleged to the Pine Barrens Tribune that Sawka has been harassing his family "for a long time." "Mr. Sawka has been a thorn in this township's side for a number of years," Bianchini told WPVI.

articles.title: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman defeats Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayor’s race
articles.summary: City Council member Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral race, NBC News projects, capping off a rapid political ascent for a progressive challenger who railed against the “broken status quo” in the country’s second-largest metropolis.
articles.body: City Council member Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral race, NBC News projects, capping off a rapid political ascent for a progressive challenger who railed against the “broken status quo” in the country’s second-largest metropolis. Raman, 45, who is part of the Democratic Socialists of America, unseated Bass, a former six-term congresswoman and a fixture of California’s political scene for decades. The result means three major cities will be led by democratic socialists, with Raman joining New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Janeese Lewis George, who won the mayor’s race in Washington, D.C., this week. Bass faced intense scrutiny over her response to a January 2025 wildfire in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood, the most destructive in Los Angeles history. The blaze erupted while she was in the West African nation of Ghana attending a presidential inauguration. It went on to destroy thousands of homes and kill 12 people. Follow live updates on the midterm elections. Raman, a former urban planner and activist, accused Bass of mismanaging the city’s homelessness problem and rising housing prices. She blasted City Hall for what she characterized as “a reluctance to move forward with the transformative policy change that this city needs right now.” Bass, for her part, argued Raman was “not ready for primetime” after six years on the City Council. The two Democrats also differed sharply on Israel’s war in Gaza, highlighting a generational split in the party. Speaking at a September forum co-hosted by the Jewish Federation Los Angeles, Raman said she agreed with left-wing influencer Hasan Piker that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians; Bass rejected that label. Raman’s candidacy drew comparisons to that of Mamdani, whose campaign rallied New York City voters dissatisfied with the political old guard. Raman touted her progressive bona fides while stressing her “independence” from the Democratic Socialists of America. The incoming mayor’s agenda will be defined in part by the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles, a complex undertaking that will test the city’s physical infrastructure, public transportation services and security systems. Raman endorsed Bass at the beginning of the year before she launched a last-minute bid of her own. Bass and Raman took the top two spots in a June 2 primary contest, advancing to a runoff over populist insurgent Spencer Pratt, a former reality television star who blasted the city’s political establishment with provocative social media videos. On the City Council, Raman represents a district that ranges from the San Fernando Valley to the Santa Monica Mountains. She was born in India and moved to the U.S. with her family as a child, later attending Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

articles.title: Harmeet Dhillon resigns from DOJ in first major postmidterm exit
articles.summary: Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice (DOJ), resigned Thursday. Dhillon is one of the first major Trump administration appointees to resign from the department and the first major figure to exit the administration after the Republicans’ midterm battering. “Serving my country as AAG for Civil…
articles.body:
Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division at the Department of Justice (DOJ), resigned Thursday.

Dhillon is one of the first major Trump administration appointees to resign from the department and the first major figure to exit the administration after the Republicans’ midterm battering.

“Serving my country as AAG for Civil Rights has been the honor of a lifetime. We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more. I want to thank President Trump for giving me this opportunity. I look forward to what’s next!” Dhillon wrote on X, using the abbreviation for diversity, equity and inclusion.

In an interview with Fox News, Dhillon said she had planned to resign for some weeks.

“I wasn’t asked to resign,” Dhillon told the outlet.

“I resigned three weeks ago, and [White House Chief of Staff] Susie [Wiles] asked me to please wait until after the midterms.”

Dhillon’s role is one traditionally focused on confronting discrimination, protecting access to the ballot and monitoring police departments found to have a pattern or practice of excessive force in their tactics.

Critics have argued she turned the role on its head.

“Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history,” Stacey Young, head of Justice Connection, a DOJ alumni group, said in a statement.

“Americans’ civil rights don’t enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it.”

A former Republican National Committeewoman for California, Dhillon was also a legal advisor for Trump’s efforts to challenge the 2020 election in court.

She also previously launched the conservative legal group the Center for American Liberty, filing legal challenges against COVID pandemic restrictions while voicing opposition to mail in ballot access.

In the months leading up to the midterms, Dhillon had penned letters to election officials warning them they could face prosecution for how they administered elections, including if any noncitizens were able to cast a ballot.

It was her division that also spearheaded the effort to get states to turn over their voter rolls, igniting a disastrous string of court losses in which the department failed in every case to gain access.

Under her watch, the department also suspended numerous consent decrees signed under the Biden administration.

According to a count by Democracy Forward, under the Trump administration, the Civil Rights Division walked away from 70 different cases and investigations into violations started under previous administrations.

The division has also launched probes into various universities, arguing they discriminated against white and Asian students.

Dhillon told Fox News on Thursday that she had “accomplished everything” she wanted to do, and waived away questions over whether she might be pardoned by President Trump.

“I have no idea. I haven’t ever discussed that with him, asked for it. And I have done nothing, in my opinion, that would require that, but, you know, that’s up to the president.”

Young noted that more than three quarters of the Civil Rights Division left under Dhillon’s tenure, arguing that “civil servants who dedicated their careers to protecting vulnerable communities were instead told to target them.”

“Dhillon wielded the enormous power of the Justice Department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court,” she said in her statement.

“She ended pattern or practice investigations into police departments and consent decrees with cities like Minneapolis and Louisville, leaving communities less safe and their residents’ rights less protected. And she refused to open investigations into ICE-related shootings, even as deaths and injuries continued to rise.”

Last December, former staffers at Dhillon’s division also penned an open letter criticizing her leadership on the 68th anniversary of the creation of the Civil Rights Division.

“We must sound the alarm about the near destruction of DOJ’s once-revered crown jewel,” they wrote at the time.

“The Administration wants you to believe that career staff who fled the Division ‘were actively in resistance mode’ and ‘decided that they’d rather not do what their job requires them to do. That could not be further from the truth. We left because this Administration turned the Division’s core mission upside down, largely abandoning its duty to protect civil rights.”

Dhillon took other surprising moves while at the Justice Department, including representing former Attorney General Pam Bondi when she appeared before the House Oversight Committee under subpoena to discuss the Epstein files.

House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) called the move a conflict of interest.

But Dhillon defended herself, saying she was there “to represent the interests of the Department of Justice” and said it was up to Bondi if she wanted to secure a personal attorney.

Attorney General Todd Blanche praised Dhillon on X, saying she led the division “with conviction.”

“She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor,” he wrote.

“The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors.”

articles.title: We all had Trump Derangement Syndrome
articles.summary: Author Jonathan Zimmerman argues that both Democrats and Republicans overemphasized Donald Trump’s influence during recent elections, leading to a significant Democratic sweep of the Senate, House and several governorships.
articles.body:
First off, nobody thought that the Democrats would score such an overwhelming victory . They flipped the Senate, the House, and five governor’s offices. And they won almost everywhere, including in longtime Republican strongholds like Texas and Kansas .

Sure, some people had predicted a Blue Wave . But this was a Blue Tsunami , and none of us saw it coming.

But more than that, we were wrong about You Know Who. Both parties radically exaggerated the power and influence of President Trump. Put simply, we were all suffering from a strain of Trump Derangement Syndrome — Republican shorthand for people who blame everything on Trump.

Sometimes, the shoe really does fit. The biggest reason for the Republican defeat was voters’ disdain for Trump. He encouraged them to pretend he was on the ballot , and that’s exactly what they did .

But don’t tell that to our reality-challenged president, who has never assumed blame for anything. “I don’t view it as a hit on me,” he told Fox News on Tuesday night, as the returns came in. “We’ve had the greatest two years in the history of the presidency.”

Yes, he really said that. And he was echoed by the soon-to-be-dethroned Speaker of the House, Mike Johnson (R-La.), who waxed on about Trump’s wonderful accomplishments. Democrats who deny them “truly do have Trump Derangement Syndrome,” Johnson said .

You know who truly has Trump Derangement Syndrome? Mike Johnson. He is so addled by it that he can’t see what Trump just did to his own party.

To be fair, not all Republicans were victims of TDS. As one Republican operative said , Trump “was ignoring what the voters were caring about” — affordability, jobs and healthcare. Trump seemed to care only about the Reflecting Pool in Washington and Jon Husted’s backside . And that’s on him, no matter what he says.

But my fellow Democrats had their own version of Trump Derangement Syndrome, which imagined him as a fascist poised to destroy democracy. And I’ll admit it: I was infected by the same virus. I worried that he would try to overturn the elections, just as he did when he lost the White House in 2020.

And I had new reasons to be concerned. Trump spent much of the last year sowing doubt about election security with further false claims about the 2020 race. And on Election Day, White House officials posted messages threatening to arrest noncitizens who tried to vote.

But federal immigration agents did not swarm voting sites , as many of us had feared. And, most of all, Trump said he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results of Tuesday’s election.

So I was wrong about that. And so were the Democrats who thought Trump’s prior victories signaled the demise of the American experiment . Conceived in liberty and hope, the argument went, the nation had descended into rancor and hate. We were irredeemably racist, sexist and homophobic. We lost our way, as a republic, and there was no way back.

That’s another form of TDS. And I hope this week’s results can cure us of it.

To be sure, Trump and his disciples engaged in plenty of hateful rhetoric during the elections. Trump repeatedly called Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed a “jihadist,” and Vice-President JD Vance suggested that Texas candidate James Talarico was gay and “obsessed” with transgender children.

And guess what? El-Sayed and Talarico both scored resounding wins. The hatred was there, but it fell mostly on deaf ears.

Talarico’s signature catchphrase was “Love Thy Neighbor,” a direct challenge to Trump’s politics of division and disdain. And it worked. We are better than the Democratic doom-scrollers thought we were.

And if you think otherwise, listen to the Republican mayor of Oklahoma City. A former member of the George W. Bush administration, David Holt wrote that his party had become “morally and intellectually bankrupt” by hitching its wagon to Trump. But there was hope on the horizon.

“It’s time to make America good again,” Holt declared.

It was always good. We just lost faith in it for a while, because Trump deranged us. I’m glad the fever has broken.

Jonathan Zimmerman teaches history and education at the University of Pennsylvania and serves on the advisory board of the Albert Lepage Center for History in the Public Interest. He is the author of “Schooling Citizens: How Education Can Save Our Democracy,” which will be published next spring by the American Philosophical Society Press.

articles.title: Horrible billionaires tax defeated in liberal California
articles.summary: It’s nice to know there are limits to what Californians can stand.
articles.body:
Well, as I said yesterday, there’s no way to sugarcoat the results of the midterms elections: it was a bloodbath for Republican candidates and a major triumph for Democrats all over the electoral map. But it was not necessarily a triumph for Democratic ideas. Their candidates won absolutely everywhere, even in deep-red states like Texas and Kansas, but their policy proposals did not fare as well.

Take, for instance, the absolutely awful billionaires tax placed on the California ballot by labor groups who were desperate to wring even more money out of Silicon Valley’s successful tech entrepreneurs. That initiative was defeated ! Imagine that: On a night where Democrats everywhere racked up double-digit wins over their Republican opponents, a quintessentially liberal idea lost in a very liberal state.

Proposition 40 was a one-time 5 percent tax on wealthy Californians, which would apply retroactively to anyone who had lived in the state in the past year. That’s so backward that it actually drove several billionaires to flee the state already. In that sense, the damage is done. Even so, it’s nice to know there are limits to what Californians can stand.

And in addition to that, Proposition 42 passed. That measure actually makes it illegal for the state to implement a retroactive wealth tax. So voters clearly did not like this idea at all. Gov. Gavin Newsom understood this, which is why he opposed the measure.

Yet far-left Rep. Ro Khanna is actually chiding him for siding with the billionaires. He wrote on X:

“All of the polling shows nearly 70 percent of Democrats support Prop 40 to tax billionaires & pay for poor kids health. Newsom is aligning with mega Trump donors Sergey Brin & Peter Thiel and Republican voters to defeat it. This is about the soul of our party.”

Excuse me, Mr. Congressmen. This is not about the soul of your party. This is about the future of your state. It’s about California becoming the kind of place that demonizes wealth creation, and thus investment and innovation. What’s made California such a wealthy state is that a lot of very smart people moved there and started extremely successful businesses. You will break this model at your peril — they will move. They’ve already proven that they will.

But this is what the far left doesn’t understand. They think people will simply refuse to respond to incentives. But the fact is, if you make it cost-prohibitive to live in a certain place, people move. The weather is perfectly nice in Florida, after all. The kind of economic climate California has enjoyed is not a certainty. Bad lefty governance can ruin it. And then there will be less tax revenue to go around.

So I hope the Democrats keep that in mind as this new majority in Congress tries to decide what its priorities will be. President Trump signals that he wants to work with Democrats to pass legislation that serves the American people. To that I say: Great. Let’s do permitting reform. Let’s build more housing. Let’s bring back manufacturing where it’s possible to do so. Let’s do everything we can to empower our citizens to live the American dream.

That is not accomplished by plundering the coffers of the richest Americans, who already pay more than their fair share. It’s nice to see some sanity out of California for a change — they did not fall for the far left’s scheme.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Nikki Haley is wrong! Democrats won midterms, Republicans didn’t just lose
articles.summary: Republicans can learn from their losses. But they should be careful not to explain away Democratic victories as if the candidates themselves had nothing to do with it.
articles.body:
Republicans are so busy explaining why voters rejected them that they aren’t acknowledging why voters intentionally chose several Democrats. Check out Nikki Haley on the “TODAY Show”: “I think for me what it was is I don’t think Democrats won, I think Republicans lost for themselves.”

Yes, Republicans have serious problems. Yes, President Trump’s approval ratings, the economy, the war and the cost of living played a role. But to reduce what happened Tuesday to a Republican rejection of Trump is to dismiss the candidates Democrats put forward and the campaigns they actually ran.

Look at Texas. Gina Hinojosa didn’t just ride an anti-Trump wave into the governor’s mansion. She became the first Latina governor in Texas history, defeating Republican incumbent Greg Abbott and ending decades of Republican control of the governor’s office.

A civil rights and labor attorney who spent years in the Texas Legislature, Hinojosa built a campaign around affordability, public education, corporate influence and the everyday concerns of working families. She connected with Latino voters by speaking directly to her roots in the Rio Grande Valley and the experiences of communities that often feel overlooked. And her argument was bigger than Trump — it spanned 20 years! Republicans have controlled Texas government for decades. She challenged voters to consider what that prolonged control had actually delivered, and they said, not enough.

Then there’s James Talarico, who won Texas’s U.S. Senate race. He resisted the temptation to get dragged into every culture-war confrontation, although everyone tried to reel him in, and instead focused on economic populism: health care costs, corporate power and the divide between the wealthy and working people. As a Type 1 diabetic, he spoke personally about the cost of insulin. He also deliberately appealed to voters of faith. He has extreme message discipline. He also understood that winning voters mattered more than winning arguments on social media.

Now, let’s go to Georgia. Keisha Lance Bottoms made history as the first Black woman elected governor in American history. But her campaign wasn’t built on symbolism alone. The former Atlanta mayor emphasized Medicaid expansion, affordable housing, higher wages, education and the cost of living. She won despite Republican businessman Rick Jackson pouring more than $200 million of his own money into the race. And there was more than a decade of intentional infrastructure that helped make Georgia competitive. Stacey Abrams spent years building political power, challenging voter suppression and expanding Democratic participation through organizations like Fair Fight Action. Bottoms’s victory didn’t happen in magically because Republicans failed — it came after years of organizing, coalition-building and political groundwork by Black women across the state.

Look at South Carolina, too. Annie Andrews flipped a Senate seat Republicans had held since 1998. She’s a pediatrician who campaigned on health care access, affordability and fighting corruption. She got criticism from her own party for being too moderate. She understood her audience and positioned herself as a pragmatic alternative. Yes, questions about nepotism and Trump’s involvement in Darline Graham’s rise created vulnerabilities. But Andrews still had to persuade voters to choose her

And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers, understanding that health care costs have skyrocketed since Trump took office and premiums are increasing by an average of 13 percent nationwide next year. He ran on universal health care being a flagship policy, working-class economics and taking corporate money out of politics.

Democrats deserve a lot of credit for these victories. These candidates built coalitions, specifically understood their states, made strategic decisions and offered voters something to vote for.

Republicans can learn from their losses. But they should be careful not to explain away Democratic victories as if the candidates themselves had nothing to do with it.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Colorado rejects ballot measure adding new restrictions on mid-decade redistricting
articles.summary: A ballot measure that would add new restrictions on any efforts to redraw Colorado’s congressional map mid-decade is projected to fail, according to Decision Desk HQ. Voters rejected the constitutional amendment, known as Amendment 86 or Initiative 256, which aimed to curb potential Democratic gerrymandering in the Centennial State after the 2026 elections by requiring…
articles.body:
A ballot measure that would add new restrictions on any efforts to redraw Colorado’s congressional map mid-decade is projected to fail, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Voters rejected the constitutional amendment, known as Amendment 86 or Initiative 256 , which aimed to curb potential Democratic gerrymandering in the Centennial State after the 2026 elections by requiring any congressional redistricting that takes place outside the typical 10-year cycle to be approved by both Colorado’s independent redistricting commission and the state Supreme Court.

The ballot measure would have also added language to the state Constitution that “the commission must hold at least three public meetings and must not adopt any plan that has the effect of dividing communities of interest or purposefully favoring one political party.”

The measure required 55 percent support to pass. DDHQ numbers show just a little more than 46 percent supported the effort. Roughly 53 percent voted against it.

Republicans and Democrats have looked to quickly redraw their House maps this cycle to add more potential pickup opportunities to their column in the fall. President Trump and Republicans encouraged GOP-led states like Texas and Missouri to redraw their House maps before November, with Democrats only being able to respond in kind in California.

Colorado is among a handful of states that uses an independent commission to review and submit congressional redistricting plans.

But both parties are already eyeing a new spat of mid-decade redistricting heading into the 2028 cycle.

Colorado Democrats were unsuccessful earlier this year in looking to pass ballot measures aimed at giving the party an opportunity to redraw their House map in time for 2028.
