articles.title: Democrat concedes in open race for Golden’s House seat in Maine
articles.summary: Democrat Matt Dunlap conceded in the open race to succeed retiring Rep. Jared Golden (D) in Maine, a statement that came around the time the Maine secretary of state’s office had announced the race had entered ranked -choice voting. “This isn’t the result we were hoping for, and I’m disappointed that we came short,” Dunlap…
articles.body:
Democrat Matt Dunlap conceded in the open race to succeed retiring Rep. Jared Golden (D) in Maine, a statement that came around the time the Maine secretary of state’s office had announced the race had entered ranked -choice voting.

“This isn’t the result we were hoping for, and I’m disappointed that we came short,” Dunlap said in a statement.

“Congratulations to Paul LePage, I wish him the best,” he continued, offering his thanks to his volunteers for helping his campaign.

Paul LePage’s win marks a key pickup for Republicans, who were looking to reclaim the seat. Golden retired after four terms in the House, and President Trump won the district three times.

The race for the state’s 2nd District headed to ranked-choice voting after LePage received just less than half of the vote.

The office said that LePage had won 170,263 votes in the initial tabulation, just shy of 50 percent, while Dunlap received 164,845 votes, roughly 48 percent. There were more than 6,000 blank votes and 123 votes for write-in candidates.

The state said because LePage didn’t outright win in the first round of vote-counting, the state would move toward ranked-choice voting on Monday.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states to use ranked-choice voting statewide.

Voters are asked to rank their choices for the office. If no candidate gets the majority of first-choice votes, the lowest-scoring candidate is eliminated and the results are retallied, using the second choice from voters whose first pick was knocked out.

Maine’s system was implemented in 2018 after voters approved it on a 2016 ballot measure .

LePage, Maine’s governor from 2011 to 2019, declared victory Wednesday, and his team asserted the Republican would have won after ranked-choice voting.

“I have spoken with Secretary of State Bellows and we are aware initial indications show a small number of blank votes and write-ins for this race may trigger Ranked Choice Voting based on their interpretation of law,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement posted to the candidate’s account on the social platform X. “It is very clear from our campaign team’s work yesterday talking one-on-one with local town clerks, and the publicly available numbers, that Paul LePage is the Congressman-Elect.”

The Hill has reached out to Dunlap’s campaign for comment.

Nathaniel Weixel contributed to this report.

articles.title: Chappell Roan’s uncle picked as Missouri House’s majority leader
articles.summary: The Republican uncle of pop star Chappell Roan has been tapped as the next majority leader of the Missouri state House, taking on the role as the GOP grapples with its worst election defeat in decades. Missouri state Rep. Darin Chappell (R), a staunch conservative who has campaigned against abortion, gun control and critical race…
articles.body:
The Republican uncle of pop star Chappell Roan has been tapped as the next majority leader of the Missouri state House, taking on the role as the GOP grapples with its worst election defeat in decades.

Missouri state Rep. Darin Chappell (R), a staunch conservative who has campaigned against abortion, gun control and critical race theory in schools, was selected Wednesday to lead the chamber’s Republican majority.

Chappell, who represents the state’s 137th House District, is the uncle of the Grammy-winning singer Kayleigh Rose Amstutz, whose stage name is Chappell Roan.

The two have notably different political views. Roan, who is openly gay and has been a vocal advocate for LGBTQ rights, previously ripped both major political parties during the 2024 presidential election, citing “ problems on both sides .” She later clarified that she would vote for former Vice President Kamala Harris over President Trump.

Her uncle, meanwhile, has supported numerous pieces of conservative legislation, including restrictions on abortion access. He previously co-sponsored legislation aimed at blocking public funding for abortion providers.

Chappell, a Navy veteran and former Missouri State University instructor, was first elected to the state House in 2022. He secured another term Tuesday with 70 percent of the vote, though his margin of victory narrowed by 15 percentage points compared with 2024.

His selection as majority leader comes after Democrats flipped 16 Missouri state House seats in Tuesday’s midterm elections, ending 14 years of Republican supermajorities in the chamber.

The losses marked the GOP’s worst showing in Missouri House elections since 1974, when Republicans lost 17 seats in the aftermath of former President Nixon’s resignation.

“We’re in a total reassessment,” Chappell told the Missouri Independent on Wednesday. “If we need to change course on specific issues, we will.”

Republicans will retain control of the chamber with 95 seats, their smallest majority since 2008, but will no longer have the two-thirds majority needed to override gubernatorial vetoes without Democratic support.

The results have prompted some Republicans to question whether the party’s legislative agenda contributed to its crushing midterm losses. Missouri voters rejected several GOP-backed proposals this year, including measures addressing income taxes and abortion restrictions.

articles.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) will no longer appear as a panelist at a George Washington University postelection analysis event Thursday, just a few days after she controversially endorsed the Republican candidate in the Michigan Senate race. Stevens was set to appear alongside CNN’s Manu Raju; Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.); Inside Elections editor Nathan Gonzales; Morris…
articles.body:
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) will no longer appear as a panelist at a George Washington University postelection analysis event Thursday, just a few days after she controversially endorsed the Republican candidate in the Michigan Senate race.

Stevens was set to appear alongside CNN’s Manu Raju; Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.); Inside Elections editor Nathan Gonzales; Morris Katz, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s campaign media strategist; and former Rep. Debbie Mucarsel-Powell (D-Fla.), who now serves as executive director of the university’s graduate school of political management.

The panel, scheduled for Thursday evening, is described as “an engaging post-election conversation featuring leading political experts.”

Representatives for Stevens and the university did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The university had previously promoted the event with Stevens, even after she endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) in the Michigan Senate race, a sharp reversal from her previous support for Abdul El-Sayed, her opponent in the Democratic primary.

Stevens’s support for Rogers was not enough to carry the former congressman over the finish line. He lost to El-Sayed by 7 points Tuesday, part of a very strong night for Democrats nationally.

Stevens was blasted by Democrats for endorsing Rogers, including the chair of the Michigan Democratic Party, who said Stevens was no longer a member and would not be in the future.

Other Michigan Democrats who criticized Stevens’s decision included Sens. Gary Peters and Elissa Slotkin, the state’s two sitting senators, as well as Rep. Debbie Dingell.

Before the endorsement, Stevens was set to appear alongside the now senator-elect at a church in Detroit just before the election in what was planned to be a show of unity and their first public appearance together since the primary.

She instead chose to appear at a church alongside Rogers after days of criticizing El-Sayed for an ad run by an outside progressive group blaming Israel for high grocery prices in the U.S. El-Sayed said that his campaign had nothing to do with the ad.

The issue of Israel and its war in Gaza was a major one in the Democratic primary. El-Sayed supports cutting off U.S. aid to Israel, while Stevens was backed by millions in outside spending from pro-Israel lobbying groups.

articles.title: El-Sayed says he’d back Van Hollen as majority leader over Schumer
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s newly elected Democratic senator, reupped his calls Thursday morning for Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) to become Senate majority leader over current Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) In an interview on “CNN News Central,” El-Sayed echoed his May endorsement of the Maryland senator for the role. “I’ve been very clear: I think…
articles.body:
Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s newly elected Democratic senator, reupped his calls Thursday morning for Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) to become Senate majority leader over current Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.)

In an interview on “CNN News Central,” El-Sayed echoed his May endorsement of the Maryland senator for the role.

“I’ve been very clear: I think he’d be an amazing Senate majority leader,” El-Sayed told CNN’s Kate Bolduan on Thursday. “Of course, that’s a choice he has to make about whether or not he wants to pursue that.

“It seems like he’s quite interested in another goal politically,” he added, in apparent reference to speculation around whether Van Hollen will run for president in 2028.

Van Hollen endorsed El-Sayed in his Senate bid — as did Schumer and other top Democratic lawmakers. At a July campaign rally, El-Sayed introduced the Maryland Democrat to a crowd of supporters as the “ next Senate majority leader .”

Newly elected Senate Democrats in Kansas , Illinois and Maine have all publicly stated they would not back Schumer as majority leader.

On Wednesday, progressive group Indivisible called for Democrats to replace their current minority leader, saying the midterm election results indicated the American public wanted a “ new generation of American fighters .”

“We need a leader in the Senate who is capable of leading that fight,” the nonprofit group wrote on social media Wednesday. “It’s time for Senate Democrats to choose new leadership.”

El-Sayed refused to explicitly say “who I’m not for” in this leadership contest and said he would examine other candidates if Van Hollen was not interested in the position.

“I am for Chris Van Hollen,” he told CNN. “If he decides he wants to be Senate majority leader, I think he’d be amazing at the job.”

“But absent him, the question for us is, all right, who are the other options here and who is going to get us to a point where we are passing legislation, putting it on the president’s desk and forcing him to make a decision so that we can talk about what we did with the mandate that we had to be able to address the affordability crisis in people’s lives,” he continued.

articles.title: Justice Department moves to toss Steve Bannon’s conviction tied to Congress’ Jan. 6 investigation
articles.summary: The Trump administration moved to vacate the conviction of Steve Bannon on two counts of contempt of Congress in connection with its investigation into the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration moved Thursday to vacate the conviction of Steve Bannon on two counts of contempt of Congress in connection with its investigation into the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. Bannon, a White House chief strategist and senior counselor during President Donald Trump’s first term, served a four-month prison sentence after the conviction in 2022. The Justice Department wrote in a court filing Thursday that it had determined “dismissal is in the interests of justice because, in an exercise of its prosecutorial discretion, the Executive Branch does not believe that it is appropriate to pursue contempt of Congress charges against a former advisor to the President who did not comply with a subpoena investigating the events of January 6, 2021, based on an asserted belief that he was protected by executive privilege.” The administration “harbors significant doubts” about the trial’s fairness, it said in the motion, which was signed by Deputy Associate Attorney General Michael Weisbuch. “President Trump has expressed grave concerns about the Biden Administration’s prosecutions related to the events of January 6, 2021, granting a large number of pardons and commutations,” the motion said. The Justice Department filing added that in light of Trump’s actions, seeking to affirm Bannon’s conviction “is inconsistent with this Administration’s enforcement priorities.” Bannon’s legal team did not oppose the motion. U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols previously denied a motion to dismiss the indictment, saying in August that the government had not adequately described why it wanted to do so. The Supreme Court had sent the case back to Nichols, wiping out an appeals court ruling that upheld the jury’s verdict. Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter previously served as Bannon’s counsel. His name does not appear on the Justice Department’s court filing. Trump pardoned hundreds of Jan. 6 defendants on his first day back in office.

articles.title: California rejects ballot measure requiring voter ID
articles.summary: A California ballot measure that would require registered voters to prove they are U.S. citizens is projected to fail, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Proposition 39 would have also required that all Californians who choose to cast their ballots by mail provide the last four digits of a government-issued ID, like a driver’s license…
articles.body:
A California ballot measure that would require registered voters to prove they are U.S. citizens is projected to fail, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Proposition 39 would have also required that all Californians who choose to cast their ballots by mail provide the last four digits of a government-issued ID, like a driver’s license number. Any in-person voting without an ID would have been prohibited.

Nearly 60 percent of voters ruled against the measure, DDHQ data shows. Just 41 percent were in favor.

The Golden State requires adults who are eligible to vote to provide an identification card and their Social Security number to register to vote.

Conservative groups like Reform California backed Proposition 39, arguing that it would increase public trust and ensure all votes are counted. The California Republican Party compared the measure to using ID to “fly, buy alcohol, cash checks, claim prizes, enter secure buildings, and prove who [you] are.”

The American Civil Liberties Union of Northern California, one of several civil rights organizations against Proposition 39, warned that providing the last four digits of a government ID outside the mail ballot envelope would have it pass “through many hands and then sit in election records for almost two years, creating real exposure for identity theft for millions of voters.”

The Sacramento Bee pushed back against the Republican state lawmakers behind the ballot measure, calling the proposition “bad policy.”

“California doesn’t have a voter fraud crisis,” the Bee’s editorial board wrote. “It has a trust crisis, fueled by national politicians — most notably Trump — who lost elections and invented conspiracies to explain it.”

Republicans in the California State Assembly tried to pass a bill last year similar to Proposition 39. Co-authored by State Assembly member Carl DeMaio (R), the bill failed to pass the Committee on Elections in April 2025.

articles.title: Division among US Democrats over Schumer’s leadership role
articles.summary: Some Democratic senators – and the very voters that swept them into power – are demanding new leadership.
articles.body:
After Democrats delivered a once-in-a-generation midterm thumping of Republicans in the United States midterms , their current leader, Chuck Schumer, has expressed confidence he will helm his party’s larger-than-expected majority in the US Senate.

“I’ll be re-elected as majority leader,” the New York Democrat told reporters in Washington on Wednesday.

But as calls for change reached a fever pitch among voters in this week’s pivotal elections, not every newly elected Senate Democrat is open to the idea of having Schumer, a 75-year-old stalwart of the chamber, reprise his role as the head of their agenda.

At least seven incoming Democratic freshmen have publicly suggested – or said outright – they will not commit to supporting Schumer in next month’s leadership vote:

Illinois Senator-elect Juliana Stratton , through a spokesperson, said she will not support Schumer.

Kansas Senator-elect Adam Hamilton told CNN in September: “I’m not supporting Schumer”.

Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson said on Monday he told Schumer he will “support somebody else”.

Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed reiterated in an interview with CNN on Thursday that he will support his soon-to-be Democratic colleague, Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, as leader.

Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan told reporters on Wednesday, “It is time for new leadership”.

New Hampshire Senator-elect Chris Pappas said in an interview last week that “voters are hungry for … a new generation of leadership in the Senate”.

Texas Senator-elect James Talarico has called for “new blood” in Washington, and since being elected, has indicated he wanted to “hear about [Schumer’s] vision” for the Senate before committing to back him.

Jackson has openly questioned Schumer’s ability to connect with working-class voters, while Flanagan’s staff has said the senator-elect wants “a progressive champion” who will shepherd Democrats through the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency and into 2028.

New members, like El-Sayed, may not be won over after Schumer backed the former public health official’s opponent, Haley Stevens, in Michigan’s Democratic primary.

Schumer, the first Jewish Senate leader, has often found himself at the centre of brewing cultural and foreign-policy debates within his party.

In remarks that were posted online in February, Schumer told Jewish leaders in New York City one of his core duties was “to fight for aid to Israel”.

“We delivered more security assistance to Israel, our ally, under my leadership than ever, ever before”, he said. “We will keep doing that.”

Schumer has also faced fierce criticism for not doing enough to block Trump’s cabinet members from being confirmed. Some have even chastised the leader for retreating during last year’s government shutdown after he backed a Republican bill to reopen federal agencies without getting anything in return.

Critics in his party, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, called that a “capitulation” that abandoned key Democratic priorities, like healthcare subsidies. Michigan Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib said Schumer should have stepped down as leader over the matter.

The Democratic leader said on Wednesday the party’s new Senate plan would include launching investigations into the Trump administration, challenging the president’s agenda and ending his war in Iran.

However, that’s not good enough for some current members, like Van Hollen, who recently told Bloomberg that Democrats should not commit to Schumer without promises of a “bold agenda”.

Before Tuesday’s election, a senior campaign staff member for Senator Jon Ossoff, who was easily re-elected to his seat, would not say whether the Georgia Democrat would back Schumer.

“I do not have an answer,” the Ossoff source told Al Jazeera. “We can do all the fantasy football stuff later.”

When Democratic lawmakers return to Washington next week, voters and Democratic-aligned groups will likely pressure them to support an alternative candidate.

After calling for new leadership after the election, Indivisible, a progressive US-based organisation that bills itself as a movement “to stop the rise of authoritarianism”, released a memo on Thursday detailing their opposition to Schumer.

“Everyone with a Democratic senator – including those with newly-elected senators on their way to DC – should be demanding a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer”, the memo read.

“Any Democrat who is considering business as usual, or unwilling to fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action – is not qualified to lead the party at this moment. Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be.”

Al Jazeera asked Schumer’s office how he plans to address those concerns and whether he is speaking with frustrated Democrats, but it has not yet responded.

To be re-elected, Schumer needs a simple majority of the Democratic Senate caucus, projected to comprise 54-56 members, and Schumer, who previously served as majority leader during the duration of former President Biden’s term in office, still has allies he can count on.

One of those is Democratic Senator Cory Booker of New Jersey, who told ABC on Wednesday that he commended Schumer’s handling of the midterms, saying he delivered “one of the most historic sweeps” for the party.

“We’re gonna have a family discussion,” Booker said. “But I think America should give … Chuck Schumer his due for what we were able to achieve.”

When asked Wednesday about building criticism of his leadership, Schumer demurred, saying Tuesday’s elections were “not about” him.

“This is about the American people and what they want and what they need and what we can do to help them. Plain and simple”.

articles.title: Tax Cuts Won and Lost in the Midterms
articles.summary: Voters punished Republicans at the polls, but their appetite for lower taxes proved more complicated at ballot initiatives.
articles.body:
Republicans received a thumping defeat in the midterm elections. As voters overwhelmingly rejected GOP candidates, they didn't outright repudiate tax policies that have historically been championed by Republicans. While some states passed ballot initiatives to raise taxes, there were several wins for fans of low taxes. Here are some of the notable outcomes from Election Day.

Voters in North Carolina approved changes to the state constitution that would cap personal and corporate income taxes at 3.5 percent. The measure, which passed with 61.2 percent of the vote, does not change North Carolina's taxes for now, but it does make it nearly impossible for the Legislature to raise taxes in the future. The state's 2027 personal income tax rate is now expected to drop to 3.49 percent, below the new cap. Meanwhile, its corporate income tax rate stands at just 2 percent, following the passage of a 2021 law that will eliminate the tax by 2030.

Voters in the Tar Heel State also approved a constitutional amendment requiring the state Legislature to impose limits on how much local governments can increase their property tax collections. However, unlike the income tax amendment, this measure does not specify what the tax limits should be. Instead, it allows lawmakers to determine how restrictive those limits should be and whether any exemptions should apply. With property taxes accounting for more than one-third of local government funding in North Carolina, those limitations are unlikely to be drastic. Still, these votes signal statewide support for lessening the tax burden.

Iowa voters approved a constitutional amendment requiring a two-thirds majority in both chambers of the state Legislature to increase corporate or individual income taxes. Amendment 1 was passed with 56.2 percent of the vote and follows years of income tax reductions in the state. In 2025, Iowa introduced a flat personal income tax rate of 3.8 percent. Free market think tanks praised the reform, with the Buckeye Institute arguing that "Iowa's economy is becoming more competitive because of the flat tax."

Although Amendment 1 does not reduce taxes, it makes it harder for future legislatures to reverse its recent low-tax reforms.

Florida was among a few states to pass property tax reforms, but the Sunshine State's were the most significant. Amendment 3 passed with 62 percent of the vote, increasing the property tax exemption on primary residences to $250,000 and halving the maximum annual increase in assessed values for non-primary residences from 10 percent to 5 percent.

While this does signal popular support for low taxes, rolling back property taxes "can be a tricky issue for libertarians to parse," notes Reason's Christian Britschgi. Property taxes are generally considered the least damaging tax to economic behavior. So the "wisdom of a property tax cut," Britschgi writes, "comes down to how local governments respond to the lost revenue and the design of the tax cut itself."

"If they respond by hiking sales taxes or demanding more state financial aid, the result would be the same-sized government, more inefficient taxes, and greater fiscal centralization. None of those outcomes would be ideal."

California voters considered Proposition 42, a constitutional amendment that would prohibit new state taxes on personal property—including stocks, business interests, and retirement savings—as well as certain retroactive taxes. The measure was particularly popular outside of the state's urban areas.

It was introduced to nullify Proposition 40, which would introduce a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires' wealth. (At press time, Proposition 40 is still too close to call.) But Proposition 42's implications are far more widespread than billionaire wealth: The measure will protect anyone with money in a savings, retirement, or investment account.

Washington voters rejected Initiative 645, a proposal to repeal the state's newly introduced 9.9 percent income tax on annual earnings above $1 million. It would also have prohibited state and local governments from introducing personal income taxes in the future. The measure was rejected by 58.12 percent of voters, meaning the millionaire tax will take effect in 2028.

Opponents of the millionaire tax made a compelling case against it, arguing that it will likely be extended to non-millionaires, too. "Not one single person we talked to believes Olympia when they say [the income tax] is not coming for them," said Brian Heywood, the founder of Let's Go Washington, the organization behind Initiative 645, at a rally in July. "They know it's coming for them."

However, fear of public spending cuts eventually outweighed fear of taxes for the Washington electorate. Activists argued that repealing the tax would "cut funding for K-12 schools, higher education and healthcare."

Oklahoma voters rejected State Question 847, a constitutional amendment that would have tightened existing limits on annual increases in property valuations used to calculate property taxes. The proposal, which was defeated by 54.3 percent of voters, would have reduced the maximum annual increase in taxable property values from 3 percent to 1.75 percent for primary residences and agricultural land, and from 5 percent to 4 percent for other properties.

Wyoming voters rejected Initiative 1, which would have slashed taxes on some residential property by 50 percent. The measure came to the ballot with more than 30,000 signatures, but 55.1 percent of voters dismissed it.

Voters rejected the measure in part because of their fear that it would result in cuts to public services. The Vote NO on Prop 1 Coalition Chair, Kim Amen, said that voters "said loudly that critical services like our public schools, first responders, road repairs, and libraries should receive the funding they need and that Wyoming families deserve."

The state had already enacted substantial cuts to property taxes—in 2025 Wyoming introduced a 25 percent exemption on the first $1 million of a primary residence's market value—so perhaps voters did not see the need for another cut .

Although voters rejected Republican politicians at elections, it isn't clear that they embraced Democratic policies either. "Voters' tax policy preferences have proven relatively stable in a period of partisan churn," Jared Walczak, senior fellow at the Tax Foundation, tells Reason. "Voters punished Republicans at the polls, but their views on tax policy seem to remain about what we would have expected in prior elections."

articles.title: Trump’s D.C.-area arch expected to be approved, but without sniper or drone plans
articles.summary: The National Capital Planning Commission is expected approve the president’s Triumphal Arch for Washington, D.C., with construction scheduled to begin almost immediately.
articles.body: The National Capital Planning Commission is expected to vote Thursday to approve President Donald Trump’s massive — and controversial — “Triumphal Arch” for Washington, D.C., with construction scheduled to begin almost immediately. The commission, led by Trump appointees, is considered likely to give the project a green light after a hearing in which scores of area residents had lined up to voice their opposition to the project, which would sit in Memorial Circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Mark Paoletta, the Office of Management and Budget general counsel who was appointed chairman of the commission in August, said in remarks at the meeting that it was a “national disgrace” that such a memorial had not already been built and praised Trump’s “monumental vision.” He said it would be “the grandest arch ever built by mankind.” The virtual meeting was interrupted for around 30 minutes during public comments by what Paoletta said was a “malicious attack” that caused the site to crash. He said it’s the “first time this has ever happened.” Close to 130 members of the public were signed up to speak, with debate by committee members and a vote to follow. “We’ll have this thing done, whether it’s past midnight or not,” Paoletta said. Opponents of the project, including the governments of Virginia and the District of Columbia, are seeking an emergency court order blocking the construction from moving forward, arguing the project is illegal. They’ve already asked a judge to immediately halt any construction in a bid to head off possible legal gamesmanship by the administration, citing its earlier destruction of the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom that includes national security measures. “It is entirely foreseeable that, once construction begins, Defendants will argue, as they have done in other cases, that an order halting construction would irreparably harm the federal government, pose security risks, and impermissibly alter the status quo they have unilaterally created,” they said. “The Court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed.” U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan has asked to be notified after the commission’s vote. Trump has said the arch would celebrate the nation’s 250th anniversary and include a military complex with drones and snipers that he said would be important for national security. The final plans submitted to the commission, however, do not mention drones, ammunition storage or sniper positions. Asked about the omission at the hearing, Greg Wischer, deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department, said the current “design is capable of hosting national security functions,” but details of those functions aren’t public and have been filed under seal in the court case. Preservationists and military veterans first filed suit to block the project earlier this year, arguing that it needed to be authorized by Congress and that the site was improper. “Its location on Memorial Circle would situate the monument on an axis between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, obstructing a line of sight that was designed to represent the unification of the Nation following the Civil War and that has existed for nearly a century,” they said. Testifying at the meeting Thursday, one of the plaintiffs, Vietnam War veteran Michael Lemmon, who served as U.S. ambassador to Armenia during the Clinton administration, called the planned arch “frankly blasphemous.” Virginia and the District of Columbia filed their own action to stop the project last week, contending it “defies at least five federal statutes,” including one that “generally limits buildings in the District to a maximum height of 130 feet.” The 250-foot arch “would exceed that limit almost twice over.” They also argued it would harm both District of Columbia and Virginia residents. “The Arch is slated to be built on a busy traffic circle that abuts the border between the jurisdictions, at the center of a historic viewshed, in a river whose environment the District has a statutory responsibility to protect,” their suit said. “Both the construction of the Arch and the completed monument will disrupt the operations of both jurisdictions, impair their ability to carry out their responsibilities under federal and local law, and require the expenditure of substantial resources to mitigate and address those impacts,” they added. In court filings, the administration countered that the city and state don’t have standing to sue and that the project was given the green light by Congress about a century ago, when it “authorized erecting and redesigning 166-foot-tall columns surmounted by statues — exceeding any applicable height limits — and those columns have not yet been built.” Attorneys for the city and state called those arguments “implausible” and said those columns had initially been planned to be built with Memorial Bridge before the idea was dropped. “As Defendants do not dispute, the Memorial Bridge Act nowhere mentions an arch,” they said.

articles.title: North Korea's fake IT worker scheme takes dangerous turn as new threats emerge every day
articles.summary: CrowdStrike says it uncovers one or two suspected North Korean fake IT worker cases daily, with operatives infiltrating defense contractors and AI firms.
articles.body: What began as a scheme to generate cash for North Korea by deploying fake IT workers at American companies has now turned into an opportunity to collect intelligence from high-value targets, cybersecurity researchers warn. New details are emerging of the sprawling spy operation within U.S. borders, with cybersecurity tech company CrowdStrike claiming it is finding one or two suspected North Korea IT worker cases every day. The scheme is creating a heightened espionage foothold inside American companies spanning multiple industries. And CrowdStrike claims it has seen remote IT workers hand off access to malware teams when North Korea identifies intelligence worth collecting. And federal cases show overseas workers gaining access to sensitive U.S. military technology. "They don't discriminate," Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's head of counter adversary operations, told Fox News Digital, explaining that the workers apply broadly across industries, from consumer companies to defense contractors. CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN But when they land inside a "particularly juicy target," Meyers said, CrowdStrike has seen the operation handed off to a malware team "because they realize that there's some intelligence value and something that they want to collect." Meyers did not say whether the malware teams successfully collected sensitive information after those handoffs. The FBI is now warning that the scheme poses a "significant national security and intellectual property theft insider threat." North Korean workers are targeting cleared defense contractors, jobs that require U.S. government security clearances, and even active-duty military personnel who can host company laptops. Recent federal cases illustrate the stakes, from a worker who successfully accessed controlled technical information at an AI defense contractor to impostors who secured offers for jobs involving military AI and Top Secret intelligence. In one case involving a network of U.S.-based "laptop farms" that helped overseas workers obtain remote jobs at more than 100 American companies, prosecutors identified a California defense contractor developing AI-powered equipment and technologies. An overseas worker using a stolen American identity was hired as a full-time remote software engineer in January 2024, according to the indictment. Instead of going to the purported employee, the company laptop was shipped to a conspirator in New Jersey and ultimately transferred to a laptop farm, where software allowed the overseas worker to operate it remotely. For more than two months, prosecutors said, the worker accessed the contractor's systems and downloaded technical data, including material controlled under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or ITAR. The indictment said documents obtained from victim companies included information related to "sensitive U.S. military technology." The same contractor hired two other overseas workers using stolen American identities within roughly six weeks, prosecutors said. Their laptops were also routed through U.S.-based facilitators for remote access. A separate case unsealed last week shows operatives pursuing positions with even more explicit national security ties. Overseas conspirators were allowed to use the identity of a Virginia man who worked for a cleared defense contractor and held an active top secret security clearance. One impostor secured a $130,000 software engineering offer at a government contractor working on a generative AI project for a component of the U.S. military. The company shipped a laptop to the Virginia man's home before discovering during a video call that the purported employee did not match the person whose identity he was using. HOW A FOREIGN GOVERNMENT HELPED ACCUSED SAUDI SPY'S FAMILY FLEE US AFTER OPENAI BUG SCANDAL Another impostor using the same identity was offered a $170,000 senior software engineering position requiring top secret/sensitive compartmented information clearance. That company caught the scheme before work began after a background investigation uncovered discrepancies and a video call revealed someone who appeared roughly 30 years younger than the man whose identity he was using. Neither impostor ultimately performed the sensitive work. But the cases show how far the operation has reached into companies handling military technology and positions requiring some of the government's highest security clearances. CrowdStrike began tracking the North Korean IT worker campaign it calls Famous Chollima in March 2024 after investigating what initially appeared to be a single malicious insider. Investigators soon identified dozens of other victims among its customers. Unlike traditional espionage operations targeting specific organizations, Meyers said, the workers cast a wide net, applying for hundreds or thousands of remote IT jobs. The primary objective is generating revenue for North Korea, according to CrowdStrike, which has linked Famous Chollima to the country's Munitions Industry Department. Meyers said the money helps fund North Korea's weapons program. But access to a valuable target can create an additional intelligence opportunity. Treasury last week sanctioned another North Korean IT-worker network, saying the regime takes most of the workers' wages and generates hundreds of millions of dollars to fund its weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs. Treasury also warned that workers have exploited corporate access to deploy malware, steal proprietary information and remove sensitive data. "The North Korean regime continues targeting and exploiting American companies through fraudulent activities conducted by its overseas IT operatives who weaponize sensitive data and extort businesses for substantial payments," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. The operation relies on stolen identities, increasingly sophisticated deception and U.S.-based facilitators who provide the physical footprint overseas workers lack. After a worker is hired, a company laptop can be shipped to a facilitator's home and configured for remote operation, making it appear to company systems that the employee is working inside the United States. Artificial intelligence is also making the deception more sophisticated. Meyers said operatives use AI to create convincing LinkedIn profiles and resumes, answer interview questions and increasingly alter their appearance on video calls. Some also use AI to help perform the jobs after being hired. The FBI says workers have purchased access to identity-verification services to test stolen identities, hired Americans to appear on camera or complete employment requirements and sometimes subcontracted entire jobs to other foreign workers. The bureau also warned that workers "almost always" remove data from victim companies because many are required to record their screens to document daily work. Federal authorities have intensified efforts to dismantle the infrastructure supporting the operation. In October, the FBI searched more than 40 suspected laptop farms across Texas, seizing 187 laptops and other devices. The DOJ said coordinated actions announced that day affected more than 70 U.S. companies. "This investigation is about far more than fraud," U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould said. "It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders." Meyers said CrowdStrike has identified laptop farms through patterns across multiple cases and passed information to the FBI, contributing to searches and arrests of U.S.-based facilitators. North Korea has also exploited the other side of the hiring process, with operatives posing as recruiters to target employees already inside companies. In a separate cryptocurrency theft investigation, Binance said a software engineer had been approached through a legitimate job platform by someone posing as an executive at a fictitious company, part of what it suspected was a North Korean effort to compromise employees through fake interviews. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Meyers said companies must treat identity verification as a security issue, not simply a hiring function, and train recruiters and security teams to recognize the tactics. "They're an employee, so they have access to whatever an employee would have," Meyers said of workers who successfully get through the hiring process. "And that could be ... the crown jewels."

articles.title: Cruz on midterms: ‘It was an a‑‑ kicking’
articles.summary: Texas Sen. Ted Cruz (R) reflected on the results of the midterm elections in his home state and nationwide, calling the Democrats’ win a “blue tsunami.” “2026 was not simply a blue wave. It was a blue tsunami. It was an a‑‑ kicking,” Cruz said in an episode of his podcast, “Verdict with Ted Cruz.”…
articles.body:
Texas Sen. Ted Cruz (R) reflected on the results of the midterm elections in his home state and nationwide, calling the Democrats’ win a “ blue tsunami .”

“2026 was not simply a blue wave. It was a blue tsunami. It was an a‑‑ kicking,” Cruz said in an episode of his podcast , “Verdict with Ted Cruz.”

The Democrats won a stunning victory in the midterm elections, securing control over the House and Senate. The party notched big wins in battleground states like Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and Michigan, flipping GOP-held seats.

In Texas, where Republicans have historically maintained a stronghold for years, Democratic candidates emerged victorious in key races. State Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D) defeated incumbent GOP Gov. Greg Abbott to be elected as the state’s first Latina governor. Abbott has served three terms, and the state has not seen a Democratic governor since Ann Richards in 1994.

The Lone Star State was also home to one of the most competitive Senate races in the country, where Democrat James Talarico defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) to become the first Democratic senator from the state in decades.

“Nowhere are the consequences of this election greater than Texas,” Cruz said in his podcast. “In the Lone Star State, we lost every single statewide election.”

“For weeks I had been publicly warning … that we were in very real danger of losing everything in Texas. Far too few believed that was possible,” he added.

In the podcast, Cruz discussed issues that led to the Republicans’ losses in the elections, highlighting the cost of living as a “top issue.”

“Food is too high. Gas is too high. Diesel is too high. Insurance is too high. Life is too high,” Cruz said. “Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long.”

He pressed the need to “listen and respond” and “champion economic policies that make a real difference in working people’s lives.”

In an earlier statement shared to social media, the Republican senator said that “Texans will be hurt” by the midterm results, which swayed the state in the direction of the Democrats.

“Their assault on business will make Texas a much less attractive place to start or grow a small business,” he wrote. “Texas will become more like California if they succeed in halting all new investment into AI.”

articles.title: Melania Trump calls for lasting Ukraine truce as she hosts Russian and Ukrainian officials
articles.summary: The US first lady was credited by all for playing a key though unspecified role in the ceasefire.
articles.body:
US First Lady Melania Trump called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine as she welcomed Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House following last week's truce in the southern region of Kherson.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.

"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.

The unusual White House event saw senior Ukrainian and Russian officials meet away from the setting of official US-brokered peace talks they have been holding without success since last year.

The delegations were made up of Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev.

Melania Trump was credited by all for playing a key though unspecified role in the ceasefire, and all parties conveyed to her the gratitude of the Russian and Ukrainian presidents.

The US first lady said she had "reviewed demining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles, and medical resources" during the truce.

"Last week in Oleshky and neighbouring areas of Kherson, people experienced the simple joys of life for the first time since 2022," Trump said. "They walked down familiar streets without fear of explosions."

She thanked both Volodymyr Zelensky and Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when the Russian president launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.

Dmitriev, a businessman and Kremlin special envoy who has previously represented Moscow during peace talks with Ukraine, thanked Trump for "saving and touching so many lives".

"Let us continue making a humanitarian contribution together; this is within our power," Dmitriev said, before gifting Melania Trump a framed drawing by an 11-year-old Oleshky evacuee.

He also praised Trump for her work on reuniting children separated from their families by the war. These include children allegedly abducted by Russia.

Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament who has also been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team, said the Oleshky ceasefire had constituted the "biggest de-escalation since 2022".

"We are creating a momentum where both sides are learning the… mechanics of how to actually keep the peace when the peace comes," he added.

He acknowledged that the "political track" of negotiations to end the conflict was "complex" but said Ukrainians were asking Melania Trump "to keep going and find new missions and de-escalate more."

At the end of the event, Trump handed Dmitriev and Arakhamia two letters to be hand-delivered to their respective presidents.

The White House later said Melania Trump had invited her guests to view two historic artifacts which she had "personally selected as powerful symbols of peace".

One was an 18th Century medicine chest which was removed from the White House when the British set it on fire in 1812. "Once adversaries, the United States and Great Britain ultimately established a strong alliance," the White House said.

The second artifact was a cup gifted in 1899 to the French ambassador in recognition of his efforts to bring the Spanish-American war to an end.

Melania Trump has generally remained discreet on foreign policy matters, and neither Moscow nor Kyiv have elaborated on the nature or extent of her involvement in coordinating the delicate ceasefire - the most enduring and widespread of the war so far.

A source who works in the local government of the Kherson region told the BBC that work on the Oleshky evacuation had been ongoing for almost a year.

However, the source said, "at a certain point other individuals became involved, seemingly after most of the groundwork had already been laid and subsequently began taking credit for the progress that had been made."

It was difficult to determine exactly who had played what role and at which stage of the process, the source acknowledged, adding that "those who had been directly involved in the negotiations for nearly a year were eventually prohibited from communicating publicly about the matter."

Speaking after the meeting in the White House had taken place, President Zelensky said the success of the Oleshky ceasefire "had proved a very simple thing: when Putin wants the fighting to stop, it stops."

"The same applies to our people who are held in Russian captivity. When Putin wants, they go home."

A source close to American officials shared a similar assessment, implying to the BBC that despite the outward praise, "the person who made [the ceasefire] possible, whether we like it or not, is essentially Putin."

"And this was done in order to pass the ball to [Donald] Trump... so that it would have some positive effect for his midterm elections."

There has been no change whatsoever in Russia's position, Ukrainian political analyst Dmytro Levus told the BBC.

Moscow "agreed to it because there was pressure from the American side... In doing so, the Russians confirmed Zelenskyy's words that, when necessary, it turns out Russia can quickly stop firing and even maintain that ceasefire."

As the frontline region of Kherson experienced its first six days of peace in several years, the rest of Ukraine continued to come under Russian attack.

This week, several drone and missile attacks killed and injured civilians across the country. On Monday alone, more than 40 people were killed in a single Russian strike on an aid distribution centre in the region of Zaporizhzhia. More are thought to still be buried under the rubble.

Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) will hold her first news conference Thursday afternoon, days after defeating incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The win ends more than three decades of GOP control of the governor’s mansion.

Hinojosa, who will become the state’s first Latina governor, is expected to outline her priorities as she prepares to take office in January. The Democrat has pledged to overhaul the state’s education policies, including replacing Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath and challenging the state’s school voucher program.

Her victory was part of a broader Democratic sweep in Texas , which also saw state Rep. James Talarico win his Senate race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R).

The event is scheduled to begin at 3 p.m. EST.

That means passing Medicare for All legislation now supported by 66 percent of the American people,” Sanders said in a video. Sanders…
articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) on Thursday called for Democrats to pass “Medicare for All” when they take control of the Senate in January.

“Healthcare must be considered as a human right, not a privilege. That means passing Medicare for All legislation now supported by 66 percent of the American people,” Sanders said in a video .

Sanders will likely be the next chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, where he will have a major platform to push for a Medicare for All agenda in the next Congress.

Progressives see Tuesday’s Democratic landslide as evidence their policies can win anywhere.

Buoyed by the victory of candidates like Abdul El-Sayed (D) in Michigan, progressives in the House and Senate are expected to make a significant push for single-payer healthcare.

Sanders said Democrats should build up to Medicare for All by immediately passing a bill expanding Medicare coverage while keeping people’s private insurance intact.

“As an immediate first step, Democrats must lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, expand Medicare to cover dental, vision, and hearing, and guarantee universal health care coverage for every child from birth through age 19,” Sanders said.

While major change is unlikely in the next two years with President Trump still in office, Sanders pushed for it to be done through reconciliation, a parliamentary procedure that lets the Senate bypass the filibuster to pass budget bills with only 51 votes.

Republicans used reconciliation to pass the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut nearly $1 trillion from Medicaid. Sanders said rolling back those cuts should also be a priority, as well as restoring the Affordable Care Act’s enhanced premium subsidies.

articles.summary: Rep. Greg Steube (R-Fla.) is running for House GOP conference chair, setting up a three-way contest with Rep. Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) and the conference’s current chair, Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.). A source familiar with the matter confirmed to The Hill that Steube is entering the race. The GOP conference chair will play a pivotal role…
articles.body:
Rep. Greg Steube (R-Fla.) is running for House GOP conference chair, setting up a three-way contest with Rep. Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) and the conference’s current chair, Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.).

A source familiar with the matter confirmed to The Hill that Steube is entering the race. The GOP conference chair will play a pivotal role in shaping the party’s messaging as Republicans move into the minority next year after Democrats swept both chambers in Tuesday’s elections.

The Florida Republican’s bid comes after he sharply criticized House and Senate GOP leadership in a post online a day after the midterms, calling them “embarrassingly weak and more afraid of governing conservatively than of disappointing the voters” who put Republicans in office.

“Instead of standing firm on our principles, you have governed out of fear, continually knelt to the moderates in our conference (who all got crushed last night anyway), and discarded conservatives like me who warned of last night’s results,” Steube continued. “Please do us all a favor and step aside so new leadership can take a truly conservative direction, with the courage to do the things we were elected to do.”

He also told Newsmax’s “Rob Schmitt Tonight” on Wednesday that he is considering running for a leadership role.

“I just don’t think that we should be putting the same people who were messaging the last two years, and we lost 30-something seats,” the lawmaker said. “Why would you put them back in the exact same positions and think that the outcome is going to be different in two years?”

Houchin said in a “Dear Colleague” letter to Republicans on Wednesday that she’s spent “over twenty years in public relations, communications, and campaigns” and that the conference should choose her.

McClain, meanwhile, touted endorsements from dozens of House Republicans, as well as two GOP candidates who were elected to Congress this cycle, in a post on social platform X.

articles.title: Rove: Paxton ‘drew down the entire Republican ticket’ in Texas
articles.summary: GOP strategist Karl Rove said he believes Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), who lost his Senate bid to Democratic state Rep. James Talarico on Tuesday, sunk other Republican candidates in the Lone Star State. “Well, Paxton drew down the entire Republican ticket. He’s at the top of the ticket as a Senate candidate, and…
articles.body:
GOP strategist Karl Rove said he believes Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), who lost his Senate bid to Democratic state Rep. James Talarico on Tuesday, sunk other Republican candidates in the Lone Star State.

“Well, Paxton drew down the entire Republican ticket. He’s at the top of the ticket as a Senate candidate, and for the first time since 1998, we lost statewide constitutional offices,” Rove said Wednesday on Fox News Radio’s “The Brian Kilmeade Show.”

“And, you have to go back to … 1982 to have the Democrats have the kind of victory they had in Texas, and we lost every statewide office,” the strategist added.

Along with Talarico, Texas Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R), who has served for three terms. And Democratic state Rep. Vikki Goodwin also unseated Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick (R), while her party similarly locked down the offices of attorney general, comptroller, railroad commissioner and agriculture commissioner in the historically GOP stronghold.

In his race against Talarico, Paxton carried notable baggage as attorney general impeachment proceedings in the Texas House related to corruption charges, of which he was later acquitted, loomed over his campaign.

Nationwide, the congressional map was also painted blue as a result of Tuesday’s midterms. Democrats secured both the House and Senate, with The Hill’s election forecasting partner Decision Desk HQ projecting their caucus will reach 262 in the lower and 55 in the upper chambers once election counts conclude.

Republicans faced an uphill battle in this year’s midterms, with the GOP weighed down by President Trump’s declining approval ratings, the cost of living and the unpopular war in Iran, among other issues.

articles.title: Nithya Raman defeats Bass to become next L.A. mayor
articles.summary: Bass conceded her loss in a phone call to Raman on Thursday. 'While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken,' Bass said.
articles.body:
Nithya Raman will be the next mayor of Los Angeles, making her the first challenger to defeat an incumbent L.A. mayor in more than two decades.

Mayor Karen Bass called Raman on Thursday to concede the race after the latest tally from Tuesday's election showed Raman with 52% of the vote compared with 48% for Bass, with 76% of the expected votes counted.

"Los Angeles, I'm deeply honored to be your next mayor," Raman, 45, said in a video statement. "I also wanted to pay tribute to Mayor Karen Bass, someone who has given decades of her life to making this city what it is today."

Bass, 73, thanked her supporters and said she accepted the decision of the voters.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken," Bass said in a statement. "I have called Councilmember Nithya Raman to congratulate her on her victory, and I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.

"Four years ago, you elected me as the first Black woman mayor in the history of Los Angeles," Bass said. "You gave me the honor of serving the city that raised me, and every single day since, I have carried that responsibility with me."

Raman's win capped off a historic sprint of a campaign. The City Council member entered the mayoral race in the final hours before the filing deadline after deciding to run the night before, going up against a onetime ally in a move that infuriated elected Democrats in L.A. who nearly unanimously supported Bass in her reelection bid.

The initial vote count after polls closed Tuesday night had Raman slightly behind Bass, but analysts saw it as a sign that Raman would win. Polls have consistently shown Raman to be heavily favored by younger, more progressive voters, who tend to turn in their ballots later than older voters.

Late-arriving mail-in ballots pushed Raman ahead, and by Thursday morning she was leading Bass by nearly 35,000 votes.

Raman and Bass were locked in a tight and contentious race up until election day, with final polling in the race showing the second-term council member and the incumbent mayor each with support from 40% of Angelenos while 19% of the electorate remained undecided.

But a blue wave across the country that toppled Republicans in the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives buoyed Raman's campaign against Bass from the left.

Raman ran with the backing of the Democratic Socialists of America, the leftist organization that endorsed Mayor Zohran Mamdani in New York and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), among others.

Bass, meanwhile, ran on a public safety message that was meant to convince moderates and more conservative voters that she was a better alternative to Raman.

The election was, first and foremost, a generational shift, as Raman swept the youth vote throughout the city and Bass performed better with voters older than 50.

"I look at this race almost completely through a generational lens," said Dan Schnur, a professor of politics at USC, Pepperdine and UC Berkeley.

"I think this is a new coalition built by Nithya Raman based on age," said Mike Trujillo, a Democratic consultant who supported Bass in the race. "This is not a geographic coalition or racial coalition, this is a when-you-were-born coalition."

The last challenger to defeat an incumbent mayor was then-City Councilmember Antonio Villaraigosa, who defeated James K. Hahn in 2005.

None of Raman's colleagues on the City Council endorsed her bid for mayor. Raman said she wasn't bothered by the lack of support, casting herself instead as a hopeful technocrat who wanted to deliver "A City That Works," her campaign slogan, promising to make L.A. a city that fixes broken sidewalks and potholes and repairs darkened streetlights in a more timely manner.

"This city's government has made solving problems look impossible for so long that I heard from people across this city who started to believe it was impossible," Raman said in an election night speech to hundreds of raucous supporters at the Greek Theatre plaza in Griffith Park. "Hopelessness can be fatal for a city, but this campaign refused to accept that."

While Raman didn't declare victory on Tuesday, her speech had all the markings of someone who expected to win.

"In just one century, Los Angeles built itself into a global metropolis," she said. "The gateway to the Pacific. A center of ingenuity and invention. The cultural capital of the entire planet. That ambitious Los Angeles, that joyful Los Angeles, that creative Los Angeles, that entrepreneurial Los Angeles, that inclusive Los Angeles is the Los Angeles that this campaign was born to fight for."

Raman's term as mayor will begin Dec. 8, and the job pays $310,000 a year. The City Council is expected to schedule a special election to fill her vacancy on the council, where she represented a Hollywood Hills-centered district.

Raman's status as mayor-elect would have seemed nearly unthinkable at the start of the year, when Bass' challengers included former reality TV star Spencer Pratt, former L.A. Unified Supt. Austin Beutner, leftist the Rev. Rae Huang and entrepreneur Adam Miller — with L.A. County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath and billionaire developer Rick Caruso also considering bids.

Beutner suspended his bid after the death of his daughter, and it seemed Bass, despite low approval ratings, might glide to a second term without a serious challenger in the race.

But the night before the filing deadline on Feb. 7, rumors began swirling that Raman was considering challenging Bass .

"She saw the lane open before anybody else. Then she got in. Once she explained to me what the lane was, I was like, she can absolutely win," said Adam Conover, an actor and writer who volunteered on Raman's campaign for mayor.

Conover explained there was a lane for a progressive pragmatist who could capitalize on voter frustration with the status quo — similar to how Raman first won her council seat in 2020, when she unseated incumbent David Ryu.

The day after Raman announced her run, Conover and others were in Raman's backyard ADU helping set up the campaign.

"Who remembers in February when it was the end of the candidate filing and no one was, like, running for mayor?" asked City Controller Kenneth Mejia at Raman's election night party. "I was like, 'Oh my God, I'm going to be here again for another four years stuck like this.'

"And then out of nowhere — out of nowhere — Nithya Raman came out of nowhere with the three-pointer and she came out of nowhere and was like, 'I'm running for mayor!'" Mejia yelled during a rollicking speech as he mimed himself shooting a basketball.

After her speech, Raman asked that her supporters join her on the dance floor, where she shimmied to "Remember the Time" by Michael Jackson, pausing every few moments to hug her backers and pose for selfies with them.

"People want change. They are not happy with what the last four years have brought," Horvath said at Raman's election night party. "They didn't want to rubber-stamp another term of it. Councilmember Raman stepped up with courage and grace to take on the status quo. It's never easy."

"It doesn't always win you friends," Horvath added, "but she did it."

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Appeals court questions if Trump’s conviction survives presidential immunity
articles.summary: A New York appeals panel questioned on Thursday whether presidential immunity or federal law bars President Trump’s criminal conviction stemming from a hush money payment made during his 2016 campaign to cover up an alleged affair. Trump’s personal lawyers said Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s (D) legal theory of the case was preempted by campaign…
articles.body:
A New York appeals panel questioned on Thursday whether presidential immunity or federal law bars President Trump’s criminal conviction stemming from a hush money payment made during his 2016 campaign to cover up an alleged affair.

Trump’s personal lawyers said Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s (D) legal theory of the case was preempted by campaign finance law and that his team wrongly showed jurors official acts from Trump’s time in the White House, including his online posts.

“Isn’t this public messaging by a sitting president, and it involves presidential communicative authority, and therefore it is directed at shaping public perception?” Associate Justice Martin Shulman asked.

“Wouldn’t that be or fit within the outer perimeter that the Supreme Court was talking about here, and therefore would have barred this stuff from coming in?”

In addition to the posts , Trump says jurors shouldn’t have been able to consider his call records while in office, his 2018 government ethics form and testimony from his onetime campaign press secretary, Hope Hicks, about her time working in the White House.

Bragg’s office says the trial was sound and none of that evidence was protected. But if the judges disagree, the guilty verdict should still stand because any issues were harmless, his office says.

It left several of the judges on Thursday questioning where to draw the line.

“If you take all of those things cumulatively, right, a problem with this evidence, there’s a problem with this evidence,” Associate Justice Bahaati Pitt-Burke said, “at what point does it not — does it stop being harmless error and turn into something else?”

Steven Wu, Bragg’s appellate chief, responded that “it would have to be a lot more than there was in this case.”

The president is fighting to overturn his 34-count criminal conviction of falsifying business records stemming from a $130,000 hush money payment to adult film star Stormy Daniels. The payment was made in the final days of the 2016 presidential campaign to cover up an alleged affair years earlier, which Trump denies.

Trump was sentenced to no jail time , though the verdict made him the first president to become a convicted felon.

The president is fighting to remove that status and destroy the case, one of four criminal prosecutions Trump faced as he campaigned to return to the White House for another term. All the others were dismissed. Bragg’s was the only one to go to trial.

Trump advances several arguments on appeal, but much of his push centers on the Supreme Court’s landmark ruling handed down after the trial that former presidents are entitled to at least presumptive immunity for their official acts.

His personal lawyers have latched on to Hicks’s testimony, in particular, that while working in the White House, Trump told her, “it would have been bad” for the Daniels story to have come out before the election.

During closing arguments, prosecutors told jurors the comment was devastating to Trump’s defense and it put the nail in his coffin. Now, it’s coming back to bite prosecutors.

“Is that so important, or was it not so important?” Associate Justice Shlomo Hagler asked.

Beyond immunity, Trump’s lawyers also argue that the case is preempted by the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA), a federal law that governs campaign finance limits. Falsifying business records in New York would be a misdemeanor on its own, but Bragg bumped up Trump’s charges to the felony version by saying the scheme involved undisclosed campaign contributions.

“There’s never been a case where a local district attorney — there’s 2,300 of them in the United States — has ever prosecuted a candidate, a federal candidate, much less a presidential candidate, for a violation, effectively, of FECA,” said Robert Giuffra, Trump’s attorney and a partner at Sullivan & Cromwell.

Thursday’s argument comes as Trump separately tries to move his appeal to federal court, hoping that he can more easily advance his presidential immunity arguments there.

The push has fallen flat so far, though the judge who has long been denying the push died late last month . His most recent rejection of Trump’s arguments is set to head to a federal appeals court later this month.

articles.title: Ro Khanna allies launch draft committee for 2028 presidential run
articles.summary: Only two days after the midterm elections, allies of Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) launched a new effort Thursday to urge the California House member to run for president in 2028. Former Rep. Jamaal Bowman (D-N.Y.) and progressive political activist Nomiki Konst are the co-chairs of the “Run Ro” draft committee, according to a news release…
articles.body:
Only two days after the midterm elections , allies of Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) launched a new effort Thursday to urge the California House member to run for president in 2028.

Former Rep. Jamaal Bowman (D-N.Y.) and progressive political activist Nomiki Konst are the co-chairs of the “ Run Ro ” draft committee, according to a news release shared with NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner.

The group, which can raise money and ramp up support for a potential Khanna presidential bid, includes members of former President Obama’s and Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-Vt.) presidential campaigns.

The California Democrat has not officially declared his candidacy for 2028, but he has openly weighed a presidential run. The Hill has reached out to Khanna’s office for comment.

NBC News was the first to report this group’s formation.

Khanna has served five terms in the U.S. House, making a name for himself by leading a bipartisan effort in Congress to pass the Epstein Files Transparency Act and for his advocacy to bring the Iran war to a close.

Bowman and Konst also cited Khanna’s efforts during his time in Congress to raise taxes on billionaires and advocate for Palestinians in the West Bank in their Thursday announcement of this group.

If successful in a presidential bid, he would be only the second person to be elected directly from the House to the Oval Office.

Bowman, who served four years in the House, called Khanna “one of the essential leaders” in the progressive movement and noted the Democratic Party’s recent victory in Tuesday’s elections, which flipped control of both chambers of Congress.

“Now is not the time to wait for progress,” Bowman said in a Thursday statement.

“With the wind at our backs after the midterms, we need a leader who puts everything on the line to fight for a better vision of America,” he continued. “That’s Ro Khanna.”
