articles.title: DOJ launches criminal probe into Supreme Court leak that exposed ruling overturning Roe v Wade
articles.summary: Federal prosecutors are probing the Supreme Court leak after Chief Justice John Roberts' internal investigation failed to identify the leaker.
articles.body: The leak that exposed the U.S. Supreme Court’s (SCOTUS) draft opinion overturning Roe v. Wade is under criminal investigation by the Department of Justice (DOJ), years after the court’s own hunt for the culprit came up empty. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s Washington, D.C., office is leading the probe, multiple sources briefed on the matter told Fox News on Wednesday. The investigation has been underway for at least a year, sources said, and comes three years after an investigation by SCOTUS failed to identify the culprit who leaked a draft of the 2022 decision. Grand jury subpoenas have been issued during the probe, though it is unclear who received them. SUPREME COURT LITIGATION FAILS TO IDENTIFY LEAKER OF DOBBS DRAFT DECISION The New York Times first reported the investigation. Politico published the draft before the June 2022 ruling, prompting Chief Justice John Roberts to order an internal investigation that failed to identify the leaker. The DOJ and the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment on the investigation. Fox News also reached out to the Supreme Court, asking whether the court or any justices have worked with outside investigators, including DOJ, or plan to do so. The criminal probe comes as Justice Samuel Alito says he has an idea who was responsible but lacks sufficient evidence to publicly identify that person. SUPREME COURT OVERTURNS ROE V. WADE IN LANDMARK ABORTION DECISION "I do have an opinion. But the evidence available at this time is not strong enough for the court or for me to say this is the person who was responsible," Alito told Fox News chief legal correspondent and "Fox News Sunday" anchor Shannon Bream in an exclusive interview last month. "It was a grave breach of the trust that everybody who worked in this building had before that point. "And it very predictably made the five of us in the majority targets for assassination and nearly resulted in the assassination of my colleague Brett Kavanaugh." Politico published the draft on May 2, 2022, revealing that at least five conservative justices were prepared to overturn Roe. The final decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization followed on June 24, 2022, ending the nationwide constitutional right to abortion. Roberts tasked Court Marshal Gail Curley with investigating the leak. After months of forensic analysis and interviews with nearly 100 employees, the court announced in January 2023 that investigators were "unable to identify a person responsible by a preponderance of the evidence." LATEST SCOTUS LEAK A GIFT TO LIBERALS ‘SALIVATING’ OVER CONTROL OF HIGH COURT NARRATIVE: EXPERTS "No one confessed to publicly disclosing the document and none of the available forensic and other evidence provided a basis for identifying any individual as the source of the document," the marshal’s report concluded. Multiple sources previously told Fox News that investigators had narrowed their inquiry into approximately 70 people who may have had access to the draft. Much of the initial focus was on roughly three dozen law clerks who worked directly with the justices. Fox News was also told at the time that Curley asked several permanent court employees who may have had access to the draft to turn over their cellphones and electronic devices. Supreme Court law clerks typically serve one-year terms for individual justices, meaning those who worked for the court when the draft leaked have since completed their clerkships. SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES Roberts brought in former Homeland Security Secretary Michael Chertoff, a former federal appeals judge, to assess the court’s investigative methods. Chertoff concluded the investigation was thorough. "At this time, I cannot identify any additional useful investigative measures," Chertoff said. The marshal’s report also found it unlikely that someone outside the court had improperly accessed its computer systems. Investigators examined court devices, networks, printers and available call and text logs without finding forensic evidence identifying the source. The report found that expanded work-from-home arrangements during the coronavirus pandemic and gaps in security policies made it easier to remove sensitive information from the building and the court’s networks. Some employees also admitted telling a spouse or partner about the draft, violating the court’s confidentiality rules, according to the report. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The leak prompted protests outside justices’ homes and deepened distrust inside the court. A California man was arrested near Kavanaugh’s Maryland home in 2022 and charged with attempting to assassinate him. "When you lose that trust, especially in the institution that I’m in, it changes the institution fundamentally," Justice Clarence Thomas said shortly after the leak. "You begin to look over your shoulder." Fox News Digital's Bradford Betz contributed to this report.

articles.title: NCPC virtual meeting for Trump triumphal arch crashes during public testimony
articles.summary: The virtual National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) meeting on Thursday to likely approve President Trump’s triumphal arch crashed after 90 minutes. The livestream went down during public testimony largely against the project and after a tense exchange with Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.). NCPC tech experts were looking into the issue, Reuters reported. The meeting resumed…
articles.body:
The virtual National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) meeting on Thursday to likely approve President Trump’s triumphal arch crashed after 90 minutes.

The livestream went down during public testimony largely against the project and after a tense exchange with Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.). NCPC tech experts were looking into the issue, Reuters reported .

The meeting resumed following a recess after the crash, and the stream was moved to the NCPC’s YouTube channel shortly after 3 p.m. EST, roughly 40 minutes after the stream crashed.

Commissioners and NCPC Chair Mark Paoletta spoke out in favor of the arch, which the Trump administration wants to build at the western end of the Arlington Memorial Bridge between Washington, D.C., and Virginia, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

Paoletta cited the 1925 congressional authorization for the Arlington Memorial Bridge Commission, which the Trump administration has cited as its reasoning to construct the arch a century later.

“I recently walked across the Memorial Bridge and walked the grounds of this empty traffic circle,” Paoletta said speaking in favor of the arch. “It is fundamentally at odds with the intent of the 1925 act, which is still in effect. It dishonors our veterans and leaves a key monumental gateway to Arlington, that Congress authorized, uncompleted. This is a national disgrace.”

Huffman, the ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, which has jurisdiction over the Department of the Interior and the National Park Service, called on the NCPC to reject the final proposal to build the arch.

“Our most revered presidents earned their place of honor,” he said during the public testimony before the stream crashed. “They didn’t try to bestow it on themselves with gaudy tributes. The monuments to them came later, after history had judged that they were deserved.”

He added, after emphasizing the lack of congressional approval on the project, that the U.S. is a “nation of laws, not kings or kangaroo commissions.”

Paoletta cited letters written by Ulysses S. Grant III, grandson of the 18th president, who wrote that Columbia Plaza on the bridge was incomplete, and asked Huffman when it was completed. Huffman argued that the congressional authorization was for the bridge, not for an arch.

“I am asking you a question, you are wrong that it’s just about a bridge,” Paoletta said.

Huffman replied that citing letters differed from congressional authorization or “legislative history.”

“I don’t think it’s going to fly, but you should try that argument in court and let’s see where it goes,” he replied, referring to the ongoing court battle with veterans and preservationists against the arch’s construction.

Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.) spoke in favor of the arch and asked if the proposal had congressional approval.

“Should our nation finish construction of a project to honor its veterans on our semiquincentennial anniversary?” Clyde said. “As a member of Congress and a 28-year Navy combat veteran, I believe the only answer to both of these questions is yes.”

Before the meeting crashed, a man named Peter Siegel challenged the reasoning for the arch’s purpose, noting remarks President Trump made last year that it was for “me.”

“That’s for the long and short of it,” Siegel said. “As far as I can tell, the National Capital Planning Commission’s mission, in its current make-up, is to realize Trump’s desire, regardless of the multiple adverse effects on national register of listed properties.”

After the meeting resumed, Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.) defended the project.

“You think about the Stars of David and those plain, white crosses across Arlington National Cemetery,” he said. “Each one of them a testament to the freedom of the United States, the service that was given to ensure the freedom of people across the United States of America, and those are the testaments to each of those lives.”

“This arch,” he continued, “this monumental arch, that is an opportunity for us to have the greatest masterpiece of tribute that has ever existed, paid to heroes of the United States of America.”

Commissioner Phil Mendelson, chair of the Council of the District of Columbia, who has inquired about specifics in the Trump administration’s proposals for the arch in the past, asked earlier in the meeting for clarification on the purpose of the project, among other questions.

Department of the Interior’s Greg Wischer replied that it “fulfills a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island.”

“But I would note as well that the [Extended Detection and Response] says that the purpose is to celebrate America’s semiquincentennial,” Mendelsen replied, later adding that he was “just trying to understand the purpose, but maybe I’ve gotten enough of an answer.”

Other commissioners also praised the arch. Paul Ingrassia , the acting General Counsel at the General Services Administration, compared the project to “a blank canvas that is long overdue and long inviting, I think, something of this stature.”

articles.title: Dem senator presses call for Kennedy to ‘resign or be fired’ after election
articles.summary: Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) renewed her call for Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to be removed from office Wednesday — more than a year after she joined fellow Democrats in demanding his ouster over the HHS secretary’s handling of the nation’s public health agencies. “The time is now. RFK Jr.…
articles.body:
Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) renewed her call for Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to be removed from office Wednesday — more than a year after she joined fellow Democrats in demanding his ouster over the HHS secretary’s handling of the nation’s public health agencies.

“The time is now. RFK Jr. must resign or be fired. End of discussion,” Alsobrooks wrote on social media Wednesday.

The Maryland Democrat has been among Kennedy’s most vocal critics in Congress, repeatedly accusing him of undermining public health by spreading vaccine misinformation and eroding trust in federal health agencies.

Her latest demand follows more than a year of efforts to push Kennedy out of the Trump administration.

In September 2025, Alsobrooks joined more than 20 Democratic senators in calling for Kennedy’s removal following a contentious Senate hearing that focused on turmoil at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and changes to federal COVID-19 vaccine recommendations.

During the hearing, the health secretary was faced with pointed questions from Democratic Sen. Mark Warner (Va.) over the number of Americans who had died from COVID-19.

When asked whether he accepted that more than 1 million Americans had died from the coronavirus, Kennedy responded, “I don’t know how many died.”

“You’re the secretary of Health and Human Services. You don’t have any idea how many Americans died from COVID?” Warner pressed.

“I don’t think anybody knows that, because there was so much data chaos coming out of the CDC and there were so many perverse incentives,” Kennedy replied.

At the time, federal and international health data showed approximately 1.2 million Americans died of COVID-19.

Ahead of that hearing, Alsobrooks had already called for Kennedy’s resignation at a rally on Capitol Hill, accusing the Trump administration official of destroying the department he was appointed to lead.

“RFK claims that he wants to make America healthy again, but from day one has systemically dismantled HHS through his anti-science, quack agenda,” she said at the time.

In February, Alsobrooks and Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden (Ore.) released a report detailing what they described as harmful actions taken by Kennedy during his first year in office. The lawmakers have continued updating the report to document his decisions as health secretary.

articles.title: Blakeman rips ‘selfish’ Stefanik after losing New York governor’s race
articles.summary: Republican Bruce Blakeman ripped outgoing Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-N.Y.) in a Thursday social media post following his loss in the New York governor’s race to incumbent Gov. Kathy Hochul (D). “Elise Stefanik is a selfish, do nothing politician that didn’t lift a finger to help Republican candidates in New York this year,” Blakeman wrote in…
articles.body:
Republican Bruce Blakeman ripped outgoing Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-N.Y.) in a Thursday social media post following his loss in the New York governor’s race to incumbent Gov. Kathy Hochul (D).

“Elise Stefanik is a selfish, do nothing politician that didn’t lift a finger to help Republican candidates in New York this year,” Blakeman wrote in a Thursday afternoon post to the social platform X.

He continued, “She had one moment of glory in what was otherwise an unremarkable career.”

Stefanik responded on social media , writing, “I voted for Bruce and straight Republican ticket and have worked for decades helping Republicans across the state and country including him.”

She cited her work for the GOP over the past decade, saying she helped to “raise over 100M to help boost Republicans up and down the ticket across the country and the state.”

“We will need everyone to be a constructive part of the effort to rebuild Republican support as we learn from this historic loss,” Stefanik concluded.

The comments came after the New York Post published an exclusive interview with Stefanik on Wednesday, in which she called Blakeman a “low-energy” candidate — adding she thinks New York’s Republican Party is “broken” and “needs to be built from scratch.”

In a separate Election Day appearance on CBS News , the House lawmaker said the results of the election were a “Republican reckoning and a Republican reset.”

Stefanik previously sought to challenge Hochul for the New York governorship but dropped her gubernatorial bid in December, paving the way for Blakeman — the Nassau County executive — to clinch the Republican nomination. She also said she would not seek reelection in the House.

The congresswoman said at the time the decision to drop out of the race did not come lightly, but she ultimately made the move to avoid an “unnecessary and protracted Republican primary, especially in a challenging state like New York.”

The outgoing lawmaker was long seen as a rising star in the Republican Party and rose to be one of President Trump’s fiercest defenders before her exit to the private sector.

Republicans were quick to coalesce around Blakeman, but it was not enough to secure him the governor’s mansion. As of Wednesday night, with 93 percent of the vote counted, Hochul was ahead of the county executive by nearly 20 points , according to The Hill’s nonpartisan election forecasting partner, Decision Desk HQ.

The Empire State GOP was able to hold on to some House seats, including Stefanik’s 21st Congressional District — which New York Republican Anthony Constantino won for his party .

Constantino, one of Trump’s endorsees, campaigned on eliminating government waste, lowering utility pricing, securing the country’s northern border and growing New York’s Republican Party, according to his campaign website .

articles.title: Where AI money worked in the midterms
articles.summary: AI-funded super PACs saw mixed effectiveness in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
articles.body:
AI-funded super PACs saw mixed effectiveness in Tuesday's midterm elections, while the newly launched Guardrails Alliance PAC, which promotes AI rules, went 5-0 in its spending. Leading the Future, an AI advocacy group , spent $4.8 million supporting Republican Darline Graham's bid to replace her late brother in the Senate. Graham lost; Democratic winner Annie Andrews dubbed her "Data Center Darline" during the campaign.

Leading the Future's other spending in the general helped propel Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., to victory despite redistricting, but Republican House candidates the super PAC supported lost, per Wired .

The other major AI-related and Anthropic-affiliated super PAC, Public First Action, spent $20 million in the general election, somewhat successfully. It backed winners Rep. Valerie Foushee, D-N.C., Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter in Ohio, Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel in Colorado, and Rep.-elect Scott Wiener in California. The Republicans backed by Public First's network lost.

Guardrails Alliance spent more than $3.1 million total opposing five candidates who lost, the group announced. But money could not buy influence on the most salient AI-related outcome of the election: local ballot measures curbing data center development, about 40 of which passed across the country on Tuesday.

The ballot initiatives coincide with hyperscalers' scramble to figure out a way forward in certain jurisdictions and overhaul their messaging around the projects.

One GOP operative told Semafor that Leading the Future was taken by surprise by the success of the data center ballot measures and had not put any resources into fighting them.

"We're proud that many of the pro-innovation champions we supported this cycle won on Tuesday," Leading the Future spokesman Jesse Hunt said. "Our investments are about building a durable coalition that can advance a national regulatory framework, unleash American innovation, and ensure workers, families, and communities are protected."

"We are committed to a multi-cycle effort and 2028 will show who actually cares about passing a national regulatory framework on AI and who wants to politicize an issue that's extremely consequential to the future of our country," he continued.

articles.title: Mississippi Senate race could head to court
articles.summary: (The Center Square) — The race for U. S.
articles.body:
(The Center Square) — The race for U.S. Senate in Mississippi is expected to end in a legal challenge as officials across the state continue to count ballots in the razor-thin contest.

Incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., and Democratic candidate Scott Colom are locked in a tight race for a seat that could lend greater strength to seismic Democratic wins in the upper chamber of Congress.

Colom leads Hyde-Smith with 49% of the vote and 96% of votes counted at the time of publication, according to the Associated Press.

Several thousand provisional ballots are expected to be counted in the race, while election officials have until Nov. 10 to resolve qualifications for those ballots. Voters can cast a provisional ballot if their qualifications to vote cannot be verified on Election Day.

Provisional ballots must contain an envelope with the voter's written and signed name. In Mississippi, provisional ballots are often referred to as "affidavit ballots."

The National Republican Senatorial Committee, which represents Hyde-Smith in legal matters, sent a letter to all 82 county election officials in Mississippi requesting provisional ballots be segregated from regular and absentee ballots. The committee also asked for officials to keep records on the status of all collected ballots and to preserve custody records for the ballots.

"As the democratic process continues to play out, we are committed to ensuring that every single lawful ballot is accurately counted and the voices of all Mississippians are heard," said NRSC Regional Press Secretary Samantha Cantrell in a statement.

Legal analysts said it is unclear whether election officials in Mississippi can comply with Republicans' request. Mississippi is one of a few states that does not have a recount mechanism or election challenge when addressing congressional races.

Candidates can, however, challenge whether certain ballots can be included in a race's tabulation under federal or state law. Hyde-Smith and the NRSC appear to be gearing up for a challenge to the provisional ballots with Thursday's letter.

"Completion of those separation and preservation processes does not eliminate applicable retention obligations. Federal law independently requires covered federal-election records to be retained and preserved for 22 months from the date of the election," NRSC lawyers wrote in a letter to election officials. "Implementation must not delay lawful tabulation, prevent the counting of any legally cast ballot, or compromise ballot secrecy."

Jessica Taylor, an analyst at The Cook Political Report, said votes appear to be trending in Colom's favor as tabulation continues.

"I think that the trajectory that it's on again unless there were some sort of court to overturn some of these ballots, I expect [Colom] to win," Taylor said in a briefing with The Center Square.

Colom's victory, combined with a potential win from Mary Peltola in Alaska, could lead to a 56-seat Democratic majority in the U.S. Senate.

Democratic leaders have also sent lawyers to Mississippi in preparation for a legal challenge to the election results. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., said she felt confident about the result in Mississippi.

"Every time we have votes coming in in Mississippi, you see Scott Colom getting more and more votes. So I feel confident there," Cortez Masto told Semafor.

Mike Hurst, chair of the Mississippi Republican Party, said the state would work to certify the election, regardless of results.

"There is no election-denying going on here," Hurst told reporters. "If the laws are followed and the voters spoke, Mississippi Republicans will have to accept that."

Mississippi must certify its election results by Dec. 10.

articles.title: LePage flips Maine's 2nd congressional district for Republicans
articles.summary: (The Center Square) — Republican Paul LePage won Maine's 2nd Congressional District Thursday when Democrat Matt Dunlap bowed out of the race two days after t...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) — Republican Paul LePage won Maine's 2nd Congressional District Thursday when Democrat Matt Dunlap bowed out of the race two days after the midterm election.

Dunlap's decision to bow out of the race came after Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows announced Thursday that the election would proceed to ranked-choice voting because neither candidate had reached the 50% threshold required under Maine law.

"This isn't the result we were hoping for, and I'm disappointed that we came short. Congratulations to Paul LePage, I wish him the best," Dunlap said in a statement. "I want to thank every volunteer who knocked doors, made calls, and made their voices heard. Your support inspired me, and I'm honored to have worked side by side with you over the past year."

"Paul LePage looks forward to working for all of the people in Maine's 2nd District. He will work with anyone, regardless of party, to put Maine first," his campaign said Thursday in a statement.

LePage will fill the seat currently occupied by outgoing Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, who decided not to run for reelection.

Trump carried the 2nd District handily in the 2020 elections, peeling off one of the state's four electoral votes. Biden took Maine's 1st congressional district in 2020 and went on to win the presidency.

LePage, a Lewiston native who served two terms as Maine's governor from 2011 to 2019, was known for his bombastic rhetoric and policies, at one point telling reporters that he was "Donald Trump before Donald Trump became popular."

He fended off a failed impeachment effort by Democrats when he was in office, feuded with neighboring Massachusetts over cross-border drug trafficking, and lost his bid for a third term against Gov. Janet Mills in the November 2022 elections after coming out of retirement in Florida.

"Maine was well served during the LePage administration, and we are grateful he is returning to public service," Maine Republican Party's chairman Jim Deyermond said in a statement. "Gov. LePage brought common sense back to the Blaine House, and now he is bringing it to Washington, D.C., on behalf of Congressional District 2. Paul LePage always puts people before politics, without fail."

LePage's flip of the seat was a bright spot in an otherwise dismal midterm result for Republicans, who lost control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate for President Trump's final two years in office.

To be sure, the firebrand former governor will be the only Republican to represent a New England state in Congress in the next session when it gets underway in January.

On Tuesday, incumbent Democrat Rep. Chellie Pingree defeated Republican Ronald C. Russell to win another term; while Democrat Troy Jackson ousted five-term GOP Sen. Susan Collins in a major upset.

The other member of Maine's congressional delegation, Sen. Angus King, an independent, wasn't up for reelection in Tuesday's midterms.

articles.title: Voters want the Iran war to end. It’s not that easy.
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said post-midterms that the conflict will conclude ‘whenever I want it to.’
articles.body: Welcome to the daily Inside Scoop newsletter. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have both said Tuesday night’s blue tsunami was a direct reflection of the American public’s dissatisfaction with the Iran war. But what does Iran think? And how does that influence what may come next? I talked to chief foreign correspondent Richard Engel on “Here’s the Scoop” about all of that. Let’s get into it. The war against Iran and its impact on the cost of living helped propel Democrats to majorities in Congress. But the conflict won’t be quick to end.
